THE BAEGAIN HUNTERS. Three women went sailing out into the street, To the brown stone front where the red flag hung, They jostled the crowd all day on their feet, While going and going and gone" was sung. For women must go where bargains are had. And buy old trash, if never so bad. And husbands must ever be groaning. Three husbands, all hungry, went homeward to dine. But when they arrived there was nothing to eat; Three women, all crazy, and feeling so fine, Were gabbling of bargains along on the street. For women must talk of bargains they buy. And homes must suffer and babes must cry. And husbands must ever be groaning. Three women were showing their husbands with glee. Their bargains at prices that never were beat; Three husbands, all starving, and mad as could be, Were tossing the bargains out into the street. For men don't know when bargains are cheap, And women, poor creatures, do nothing but w eel), And husbands must ever be groaning.
merican Paper.

A JAPANESE LEGEND. When the dogs of war were at large And all the land at strife A loving flume took her infant charge And fled to save his life Fled to the mountains away. With eager step and look; And there for many a day They dwelt in a hidden nook. Dwelt secure, till at length Both child and nurse must die With dimming eye, and with failing:strength, Within the cave they lie. trace they leave behind; For the outer world to tell Where their bodies to seek and to find To give them burial. And years have passed since then, Yet the mountain's depths are stired;

At the midnight hoar. airain and wain, A wailing sound is hearth And the traveller listens with drE ad, For he knows that murmur wild Is the voice of one who has long lain dead. Calling her dear lost child.

THE FATIIERE BIRTHDAY. Heart of mine, why beat so quickly? Brain, why throb with fever heat? foul, why art thou so dejected? Mem'ry, why sad tales repeat? Eager thought, why now so tardy? Why with hesitation stay? Let, oh let thy brilliant sunrise Chase the gloom of night away Now I need the inspiration Thou, my fitful muse. canst give; 'Words I need to tell a Father, How I wish he long may live. Right are they who hold that language Cannot, fully, thoughts impart, When the tongue would well and truly Speak the language of the heart. 'Yet the language of affection Garb'd in simple words maybe, Say I then, with heartfelt fervour, "God grant all I crave for thee I" Joy and peace in true believing, Faith, hope, love, and grace divine; Health, long life, and choicest favours, Choicest gifts of God be thine :

Over all unpleasant bygones May oblivion throw a pall; May fond memory, with rigour,. Scenes of happiness recall I He from whom all good prOceedeth. Hath been, and will be. thy Friend, He bath been thy loving-Father. He will love thee to the end! Ne'er may doubt or fear annoy thee, Trust in God's unchanging love, Live on earth anticipating Life of endless bliss above EDWARD N. MARKS.

div.head: Varittito.
div.p: Varittito.

A fondness for tales of fiction has characterised most of the great minds in history. It is the fear of things that never happen that causes half the misery from which we suffer. The three most inquisitive English rivers, according to cockneys,—the Wye, the Wen, and the Ware. We might enjoy much peace if we would not busy our- selves with the words and deeds of other men, which apper- tain not to our charge. Jones complained of a bad smell about the post-office and asked' groan whit it could be. Brown didn't know, but sug- gested it might be the dead letters. The izirate is a very timid animal. His neck is so long that when his heart comes in his month it takes him half a day to get it bacit where it belongs. "Grai.dma, why don't von keep a servant any longer ?" "Wetl, you see, my child, I'm getting old now, and can't take care of one as I used to do, you know." Feverish haste to be rich, avidity after that which is sen- sational and startling, superficial reading—these make the so.iiety of the present like a hasheesh dream. To do an evil action is bass; to do a good one without in- curring danger is common enough; but it is the part of a good man to do great and noble deeds though he risks every-

thing. The 'home is the sunniest side of every great people. Without devotion to home there can be no devotion to coun- try. The home is the cradle of good citizenship and patriot- ism ; it is the fountain of happiness, not only to individuals, but to nations as well; and it is the one spot on earth that should be guarded from needless shadows. Louis XVIII. told one of his courtiers one day that be was in the habit of asking his Ministers whether they had a majority. When answered in the affirmative, he would say —"Very well; then you don't want we, and I can go." if the reply was in the negative, he would observe—" Very well ; then I don't want you, and you can go." An ignorant fellow, who was about to get married, re- solved to make himself perfect in the responses of the mar- riage service; but by mistake he learned the office of bap- tism for those of riper years; so when the clergyman asked him in the church, •' Wilt thou have this woman to be thy wedded wife?" the bridegroom answered, in a very solemn tone," I renounce them all." The astonished minister said, "I think you are a fool." To which he replied," All this I steadfastly believe." A TALKING CANARY.—It is stated, on the authority of Mr. W. li. Shrubsole, F.G.S.' of Sheerness, that a canary bird, belonging to a shepherd named Mungeam, living at Scraps-gate, near Sheerness, is able to utter words and sen- tences so as to be readily understood. Sometimes the bird interpolates phrases in the middle of a song, but it is heard to better advantage when it speaks, as it often does, with- out singing. So far as can be ascertained, there is no re- cord of a similar ornithologicallaccomplishment.—Times. One day, a number of probationers had met in the Pres- bytery-house. Jamie, who happened to be there, drew out a pictorial pocket handkerchief. "That's a braw napkin ye've got, Jamie," sail one of the young men. "Yes, man," said Jamie, spreading it out at the same time. "That's Louis Napoleon .in the tare corner, an' that's Victor Emanuel In the tither; an' here's Bismarck in this corner, an' Count Cavonr in that; an' that's her Majesty the Queen in the middle. The fac' is, I never get my nose intae gods so- ciety except when I blaw't." YOILA AND LANCASTER ROSE—The true York and Lan- caster we believe to be a striped damask rose; but there is another that often bears the name, the proper name of which is Rosa mundi, and its alliance is with the French roie (Rosa Gallica). These are not the only striped roses known to cultivators, for in truth there are many; but not one of the throng has ever been much prized by critical enthusiasts —that is to say, by rosarians, for that is the fashionable de- signation of the modern posonAniacs.—Fanziliar Garden

Flowers. Tam ARTIST'S PRACTICAL JOICE.—We have an anecdote of Pierre Mignard, illustrating the powers of copyists and imitators. This French painter procured an old Roman can- vas, upon which had been painted a portrait of a cardinal ; over this he painted a "Magdalen" in the style of Guillo Real. He then arranged matters with a broker, who, I'M- parting as a secret to the Chevalier de Clairville that he was to receive from Italy a specimen of Guido in his best ,time, effected its sale to this nobleman for 2,000 crowns. After some time, Mignard himself, whose main object in this affair seems to haSe been to affront Charles Le Brun, spread about a rumour that the work was a fabrication of his own; but all the critics were agreed upon its undisputable genuine- ness as a picture by Guido. To end the matter, the Cheva- lier invited Le Brun, Mignard, and several of the foremost connoisseurs to dinmar, when the question of the authorship of the picture was again brought forward. After a most rigorous examination it was finally declared to be a master- piece of the Bolognese master, and of his very best time. .A violent dispute arose between Le Hutu and Mignard, to end which, the latter' offered to remove part of .the Magdalen's hair and display the picture underneath. After some demur on the part of the Chevalier, who doubtless clung to the belief in its authenticity, this was at length agreed to, and lot a caxdinal'', Cap met their as ! This of dourse settled the question, and Mignard was congratulated upon his skill and approximation of the manner of the great master, when Le Brun, much vexed, sarcastically exclaimed' " Always paint Guido, and never paint Mignard ! .as pastures known by the A PLaotta or Ssaits.—When at L tbourne a fortnight oavgered so thickly with soul" achgoa,rmlinfgoannadniteheof finpearaadisnclulae"tci striped snails that it was impossible to set a foot down with- out covering several of them. I sent a few specimens to Miss °ramrod, of Danster Lodge, Isleworth, and was favoured with the following remarks in relation to them : " I believe your snails found in large numbers ort a pasture at Eastbourne are the Helix virgeta (Da Costa). Jeffreys' vol. 1, pp. 210 to 213, mentions that remarkable for appearing in vast numbers, 13hriesti on the stalks of grass, or leaves of shrubs, and are especially eshsn Caoilsnch are ology noticeable when rain incurs after; dry weather. They are mainly found near the sea coast, and are so numerous in South Devon and on the fine short grass on sand hillocks near the Land's End that the sheep cannot avoid eating them in great quantity, and the delicate taste of the Dart- moor and Cornish mutton has been attributed by various writers from the time of Borlase, 1758, onwards to this item of their diet. Your specimens have been so crushed in the post that I cannot feel certain whether they are this species or H. ericetorum (Muller), which is very like it (even with type specimens before me), but my sister, Georgina Orme- , rod, who has an excellent knowledge of English shells, will be able to say with certainty when she !returns on Friday evening, and I will then just send a line." In reference to garden vermin generally, Miss Ormerod observes :—" I have hal very great success for more than a year now in keeping down 81u45 and snails, and plant vermin generally, by plen- tiful use of gas-lime—of course, used with care according to _

its condition. A Nzve Causer.— A churn of Canadian manufacture, called 4. The Figure Eight," has been exhibited at work by Mr. Clayton Slater at Skipton, in the presence of several agriculturists and others interested. This churn, as described by the Okaven Herald, is of a simple construction, but of a totally different form to those hitherto in use. Owing'to its peculiar mechanism, a high rate of velocity is given to the cream, and anothi r important feature is the simplicity and pen ection of its ventilation, a current of air continually passing through it by means of two bell-mouthed tubes, reeds of tin, waich are placed in the lid. In the centre of the lid a carcase piece of glass is inserted, by means of whieh the preserce of the butter is at once observed. An- other improvement is the ease with which the butter can be I separated from the buttermilk. Half a revolution of the wheel is sufficient to place the butter at one end of the barrel, when a wooden strainer can be inserted, amlthe mo- tion being reversed, a plug is withdrawn from the bottom and the buttermilk runs ont.=The washing and brining is done by the same process, and the butter is taken out by means of a large wooden spoon. The experiments were not carried out under the most favourable circumstances. The 1 bearings of the churn, which are of wood, were somewhat strained, and interfered with the free working of the dif- ferent parts, and the handle of the driving wheel snapped off just as the operations commenced, so that the motive power had to be supplied by a man at each end of the barrel, pushing and pulling it backward and forward. Mr. Slater first of all scalded the barrel with hot water, and this having been ran out by the withdrawal of the plug, about two gallons of cream, which was tested by a thermometer at 62 degrees, was then Routed in. This lot-was rather of an inferior quality, and weighed 191 b. lloz. The churning then commenced in the laborious manner described above and 51b. 7oz. of butter was produced in four minutes forty seconds. The batter was then removed in the manner men- tioned previously, Mr. Slater canine attention to the fact that there was no necessity to tenant with the hand. The darn was then again thoroughly scalded out, and a fresh supply of cream poured in, anti 'Titles. of butter produced from 191bs. 4oz. of cream in three minutes twenty-five seconds. This time although very good, would doubtless have been shortened by half a minute had the churn been in better working order, as was exemplified by a previous trial at Barnoldswick, when Mr. Slater obtained 101bs. 30z. of butter from two gallons of cream in about three minutes. AN EGG ROILiNCE.—A Williamsburg grocer tells this story of the strangest hatching ever brought forth froraean egg:—lt was on Saturday night, I think, about two months ago. There was a great rush of customers, and our girl, who is very handy, came down Stairs to help us in the store. Well, that day I had bought five barrels of eggs from acom- mission house in Duane-street, near Greenwich, New York. They had come from Tennessee. One barrel was used up when the girl came down, and I had just opened another. he began to sell from this barrel. About fie minutes later I heard her laughing, and saw her holding an egg to the light. She looked at it so intently that I drew near and asked if it was bad. "Oh, no.' she answered, " It's too good." She handed me the egg, pointing to some words written upon it in a clear, business-like hand. They were as follows:—" Will the young lady in whose hands this egg Way fall open correspondence with—, County, Ten- neesee ?" I read it aloud, and a lady who !chanced to be present, said, "flow romantic!" I thought so too, and we ‘l.l had a good laugh over it. After the shutters had been put up I told the girl, just for the fun of the thing, to com- ply with the request on the egg, and send;aletter to Ten- t,nessee. Before going to bed she did so. She is well edu- dated, and writes an excellent letter. She was brought up in a convect in Ireland. Well, to make a long story short, he proposed by letter, and Was accepted. On Thurs- day last he arrived from Tennessee and saw her for the first time. • They were mutually pleased, and the wedding day was eet fer some time in the middle of August. It is a good ,match, and I hope they will be happy together. "Is our :friend from Tennessee in good circumstances ?" asked the ireporrer. "Oh, yes," replied Mr. Lynch, "I forgot to tell. you. He owns considerable land, and is quite well-to-do ;He is also a large shipper of produce, and just out of fun he 'wrote the message on the fatal egg. He knew the eggs would be chipped to New Yor'a, but they might have been sent from this city to Europe, or anywhere else. He was so pleased with the answer to his message that he made up his mind to marry the girl who had written it, if her appear- ance pleased him. It would have been strange if it had not, for she is a remarkably handsome girl, not yet 20 years old, with a fine complexion, large brown eyes, and a grace- 'fill abeam. She is also as amiable as she is pretty. He is a finelookin; Mall, about 30 years of age, and they make a hanimme couple I can tell you." Piave...Yr Courisnes IN ALIStP, SHOWERY WEATHER. Let me endeateour to deal with the subject in detail, and in the first place ask what is the best course to take with wheat featly ripe for cutting when the weather keeps damp and showay ? Some may reply—allow it to remain unmet as long es possible, trusting that the weather will change; but by no ding the grain, as well as the straw, will be sure to deter orate, the former by becoming coarse in the skin and dark coloured, the latter in contracting mildew, while the crop altogether has the liability el being beaten down by 'adverse storms, and of entailieg more labour and expense on the cutting. I should rather counsel that the reaping ma- chine be kept continuously ein action, the entire labour 11 strength of the farm being employed in tieing the grain I after iato sheaves, never halting in this unless it be too damp to be tied, placing the sheaves in stooks immediately, or, should they require little or no conditioning, building them at once into small wind-ricks, with about a waggon load of shelves in each one of them. The chief reason why this recommends itself, apart from weather considerations, is that the system dovetails well into that of early threshing during rr soon after harvest, which in these needy times seems to be so generally in favour. Well made wind-ricks keep the wheat in better condition than larger ricks. Country people used to imagine that the wind blew quite through them, hence, probably, their name. No doubt the dry air circulates through them readily if the wind does not; and, while in the wettest weather the rain drips off from the outsides, failing to enter, whenever better weather comes the grain gets into Very dry, healthy condition within. Any good workman, skilled in building other stacks, would find no difficulty in performing the work with a few simple instructions. The foundation would be about forty 1 or fifty sheaves placed quite upright in the centre, and only slightly declining at the outside. On this the stacker would build round and rotted, binding the sheaves tightly together as he proceeds, and always keeping their crops towards the centre and their bats reclining outwards. The best form swells a little at first as the rick rises from the ground, but only for a brief space, after which it is brought tapering up to a point, and if a couple of reed sheaves were spread over this there would absolutely be no sheave-tops whatever ex- posed. But what is to be done with barley when the weather keeps damp and showery?' This grain, it is well known, germinates very quickly, and grievous complaints have already been made since the harvest commenced of barley crops which had been expected to yield valuable grain for malting purposes having been completely spoiled through lying on the ground in the wet and growing Out. But why permitted to lie on the ground? I contend that under such circumstances barley ought to be treated pre- cisely as wheat, in being tied into sheaves and placed into wind-ricks. An old farmer of the West of England, who Was more successful than any of his neighbours in harveeit- ing his corn without damage in bad weather, was once asked what his secret was. He merely replied, " Always keep the corn up on its legs," by which he meant that only the bat ends of the sheaves should come in contact with the ground. I believe in this thoroughly, for if the land is wet and ears of corn be allowed to lie on it unmoved for even a very short period they will be sure to sprout. But Igo further than this, maintaining the utility not only of having all corn sheaved in had weather and kept well off the ground, but of packing it securely out of the way of damage from any of the elements into these easily constructed little wind- ricks. THE HAND OF THE LORD AND THE HAND OF MAN.— When the other day Mr. C.. 8. Read said that it was "better to fall into the hand of the Lord," he did not anticipate that that hand would be so heavy upon farmers daring the present harvest. But "what can't be avoided must be abided," and the main truth still remains, that a spirit of discontent against hardships caused by the hand of man may welt be called—as it was by the late Mr. Kingsley— "divine ;" whereas a like spirit indulged against irresistible Erovidence would be both useless and wicked. The writer well remembers meeting, on that dreadful Tuesday of the Kilburn Show, a member of the Royal Council, who had a smile upon his face, apparently expressing his fall satisfac- tion with everything. And yet it was pretty well acknow- ledged then that not only would the show be a financial disaster to the society, but a source of present discomfort and dissatisfaction to its members and visitoia. This mem- ber of Council not only said that there was nothing for it except laughing or crying, and for himself he preferred the former; but he also acted as if he and his coadjutors, hav- ing done their best, ought not to give themselves any useless anxiety. This no doubt is the proper spirit for us fariners to maintain, if it be possible at the present time. The bulk of us are ordinary men, full of faults and failures, and even, if there be amongst us here and there a Paul or an Apollo, still the " increase" depends upon a higher power than that of him who may plant or him who may water. Bat quite a different course of conduct is not only desirable but neces- sary when we" fall into the hand of man." Resignation, which in the one case is both worldly-wise and heavenly - wise, is in the other case a fault; nay, not simply's crime, but a mistake. No reform was ever yet inaugurated, much less carried out, without active-signs of discontent amongst the reformers. Nay, more. ,No reform has ever yet been carried out unless those who suffered themselves lent a help- ing hand. " Who would be free himself must strike the blow." I will again quote Mr. Read: "There are many cases that he knew of where the tenant bad had to pay an increased rent because of the improvements he had made on his farm." Just now it is the fashion to say that such cases occur in Ireland, but not in England. But it is high time that the sense of justice which is said to be powerful with Englishmen should be directed and thoroughly awakened to the present condition of the English tenant farmer. It has been, unhappily, said that tenant-right carries with it land- lord-wrong. At present the wrong has been pretty much borne by the tenant, and it remains with the tenants to right it. It will not be done without their action. Let them make up their minds to ask Parliament, with no uncertain voice, to give to each man a right of property in that which' he has himself created, and then property will soon be made more sacred than it yet is. But if tenant farmers continue to stand waiting for "something to turn up," or" shut their eyes and open their mouths and see what will be sent them," the only thankfulness they are likely to feel is that ..ftme thankfulness which they have often expressed, for nothing. —T. C. S., in Agricultural Gazette.

A CortsxuvArtvE ESTIMATE OF THE DURHAM AND LIN- COLNSHIRE ELECTIONS.—The Standard says: Sir Stafford Northcote must know perfectly well that no greater calamity could befall the Conservative party than to take office upon such a programme as that which is definately foreshadowed in Mr. Lowther's speeches in North Lincolnshire. and a little less definitely in Sir George Elliot's appeals to the electors of North Durham. If, however, the Conservative party are not prepared to return to protective duties, then neither the election of Mr. Lowther in North Lincolnshire nor that of Sir George Elliot in North Durham can be, with- out qualification, spoken of as Conservative victories. Thus while the Government cannot afford to disregard the signi- ficance of the two defeats which they have eustained, the Leaders of the Opposition cannot recognise in them ground for unalloyed satisfaction. Will they not rather feel that the issue on which the electoral contest in North Lincoln- shire and North Durham have been fought and won are pregnant with the causes of embarrassment and perplexity. A PRAYER OUT OF SEASON.—A Correspondent writes : " They seem to do things strangely in Wales. In the course of my tour I came to Abergele-cum-Pensarn, one of the gems of the principality. I was grieved to find that the 'plague of immoderate rain and waters,' which threatens the future of our agriculturists, had been very serious here. Towards the end of the week a 'seasonable and blessed change of weather took place. This was a source of joy and hope to all. On Sunday morning I wended my way to a church not ten miles oftwith thankfulness to Almighty God for His mercy, and looked forward with gladness to the Thanks- -giving for fair weather.' But, alas! I was bitterly disap- pointed. The officiating clergyman at the place appointed with great fervour thanked God in that it had pleased Him, in our great necessity, to send us, at the last, a joyful rain to refresh His inheritance when it was dry.' What mockery ! If this is an instance of what the Welsh clergy do, it is no wonder that the church in Wales has lost her hold upon the people." W. HAMILTON. SUNDAY HAEVESTING.—At the Ulverston Parish Church, on Sunday morning last, the vicar, the Rsv. C. W. Bardsley preached a sermon upon Sabbath observance. Alluding to the strictness of the Judaic law regarding Sabbath obser- vance, be pointed out that what was practicable in the wil- derness inn hot clime, and where manna was rained down for the sustenance of the dwellers, was quite impossible in colder climes. When be was resident in Manchester the thought of leading hay on a Sunday would have been re- garded by him as an infraction of the Sabbath; but since he came to Ulverston he had seen the matter irl a different light. He had frequently been asked this summer by farmers did he consider it a sin to get their hay secured on a Sunday. He thought the matter out, and he felt that whilst the Fourth Commandment was applicable to the dwellers in the wilderness, its strictness had been abrogated by our Saviour" Which ot you have an ox or an ass," &c. Christ performed most of his miracles on a Sunday, and the • Sadducees were awfully offended. He allowed his disciples ' to gather and eat wheat on the Sunday, end the Sadduceis were wroth. Plainly, that Christ gave His sanctioo that works of necessitror works of mercy could be performed on the Sabbath. Putting aside the loss or profit to the farmer as to whether his hay was secured in good or bad condition, he (Mr. Bardsley) held that it was an act of mercy to secure it in good condition ? mercy to the live stock that had it to eat, and so they would tell us if they could speak. He ‘thus held that in a season Of bad weather the farmer who secured Isis bay on a Sunday performed but a simple duty where the necessity existed.—The Mark, Lane Express on the same subject says :—" On Sunday week, August 23, a very large proportion of the outstandfng wheat crop in the south of England was in fair condition for in-gathering, owing to the strong winds which prevailed during the two previous days, hut Sunday harvesting is very exceptional, and consequently but a small percentage of this valuable proportion of the out standing crop was saved from the disastrous effects of the deluge of rain which fell on Monday night and during Tuesday.

FREE TRADE. Sin,—The fable is, the Devil was under a wall when a man was passing; he said to him, "You see that old woman in the apple tree stealing apples; she will fall shortly and blame me for it." Down the woman came, and cried that the Evil One was in it. He then said, "This is the way people blame me when I am innocent; you know that I had nothing to do with it." So it is with certain classes in this country if anything disturbs trade and slightly checks its progress; good, innocent Free Trade has to bear all the blame. But to these charges it pleads not guilty, and when tried in a court Of justice it is acquitted, and leaves the court without a stain on its Character. Men, in their eager- ness to get money, disturb trade, check its progress, and then, instead• of blaming themselves for it, cast all the blame on Free Trade, and try to their utmost to bring it Into disrepute. ' A few years since coals sold at an enormous price; nothing was so profitable as a colliery; it was and would be a mine of wealth; its owners would 'have abundant riches, roll in them all their days, and leave them in such abundance that their children would have high positioniand every enjoy- ment. Men of all classes who had money or no money, wishing to be rich, were carried away with these dreams of gold, and rushed into the business, opened new collieries and enlarged old ones, and caused the supply of coal to be greatly in excess of the demand; colliers' wages were tabu- lonely high; they had by far the least work and the highest wages of any class of workmen. . What is more essential to the well-being of man than water? What is so cheap? Why? It is most abundant. Who can keep up prices when the market is over-stocked, or when the supply is in excess of the demand ? It is not in the power of any man, or of any combination of men, to do It. Men who supply the market with coal and who get it have done their best to maintain high prices, to make large profits, and to keep up wages. But it cannot be done; they have failed. It would be as easy to stop the rain from fall- ing, the wind from blowing, and the sun from shining as to do it. Supply and demand are omnipotent in the market; they fix the price; we are in their hands, and must submit to their power. The rush to be rich by coal mining has caused hundreds of thousafids of pounds to be lost, and many colfieries to be unprofitable. Coal mining is not alone in this respect; it is a type of other industries. The building trade, the iron trade, and many others have suffered from the same cause, and with the same results. Bad seasons at home and famines abroad have diminished the power of the people to purchase and seriously affected trade. Wars iand rumours of wars have caused the spending of millions of money with as little profit to the country as if it had been sunk la- the sea. These things have checked trade; it could not be otherwise; for money lost in speculation, thrown away in wars, and taken out of trade by dear provisions, must, in the nature of things, produce bad trade and all its results. Free trade has not been to blame for the checks we have had; and, in all honesty to ourselves and others, we should find out the cause or causes, and not blame the Innocent. ' How about the agricultural interest? Has it not suffered by Free Trade? It has not. How can it be that it has suffered by it when the rental of the land of this country is over £30,000,000 per annum more than it was when we adopted Free Trade ? Taking the landowner and farmer together, it has greatly benefited them. But still the fact remains that farmers are depressed. True, but not by Free Trade, but for the want of it. They are living and work- ing under a system of oppression and repression, and while they do this the owners of the land will, to a great extent, reap the fruit of their skill and toil? and continue to grow rich at their expense. Free Trade in land and proper se. eurity for, the outlay of their 'money and skill, would lift them out of all their difficulties and make them a prosperous -people. They are in chains ; but they have the power in their own bands to snap them asunder, and to stand before the world free men, rejoicing in Free Trade. J. W. Preston,_ Aug., 27tht 1881.

CONTINIIOI7S CORN Cisownro.—Mr. Clare Sewell Read has contributed an article on "Continuous Corn Growing" to The Squire, which is to appear in the September number of that magazine. The demonstration given in Mr. Front's recently published treatise of the profitableness of his clay farming and his assumption of the suitableness Of his meth6d to clay lands in general seemed to Mr. Read to stand in some need of modification. Mr. Read therefore checks Mr. Front's statement by a narrativituf his own seven years' experience in trying to hring the theory of continuous corn growing into successful practice on a clay soil In his own county. The result is, to quote Mr. Read's words, that "it has succeeded both in experimental plots and upon a large farm in Herta, but failed in Norfolk. Rothamsted, where Mr. Lawes has conducted a long series of scientific experi- ments, and Mr. Primes farm, Sawbridgeworth, are both in the same county, the soils may be similar, and they pro- bably both rest upon the same geological formation. What may suit one soil or one locality may not succeed in another. The moral that I draw from my clay farm is that the ex- tent of land adapted for continuous corn growing by the aid of light mannres is more limited than some recently pub lished experiments would lead us to imagine." A TERREsTister, PARADISE.—The predominant feeling in my breast as I traversed a part of what the late Earl of Beaconsfield termed the" illimitable wilderness" of Western I Canada was deep regret that such a regon should remain untenanted by busy men. There, year after year the sum- mer sun floods with warmth millions of acres where beauti- ful prairie flowers bloom and wither, and nutritious grasses spring up aud decay. The snows of winter cover the earth with a garment which, though apparently a cold shroud, is really a warm mantle. Game breeds and dies without yielding food to more than a few hunters. Fish spawn and fill the lakes and rivers without being utilised to vary or constitute the substance of more than a few Indians. When I thought of the millions of people who might be fed and rear families on the untrodden prairies, and enjoy the game and the fish which abound, it saddened me to contemplate the neglect with which Nature's banquet was treated. And the sadness deepened when I reflected how many landless millions in Europe were struggling for the necessaries of life, or were longing to be the possessors of land which they might call their own, whilst food was easily procurable here by all who might desire it, and land could be flied for the asking by all corners. I haye seen a large part of the North American continent. I have marvelled at the enterprise which has converted so much of it from a wilderness into a garden. No other tract can so easily undergo the same transformation as the Canadian Far VVest. I cannot believe that it will long remain unappreciated and unpeopled. . . Any citizen of the British Empire can get a farm in Man- itoba on very easy terms. The Canadian Homestead Act provides that he may secure 160 acres of land on payrag an office fee of 510, living there three years, erecting a dwell- ing on it not less than 18 feet long by 16 feet wide, and cultivating a Dart of the land. On complying with these conditions, he becomes absolute owner of the land. His task his not hard. He may grow a crop the first year of occupa- tion which will reimburse him for all his outlay. Should he have cattle, they can graze free of cost on the prairie grass; and be fed in winter on hay which he obtains for the trouble of cutting and curing it. In order to succeed he must start with capital; the minimum sum which he ought to have on beginning to farm fs 5500; the larger his capital the greater his chance of success. In any ease, he must make up his mind to endure some privations, to eat very plain food, to sleep little and work very hard. Should he be diligent in toiling with his hands, he may count on being in comfortable circumstances at the end of five years, and a rich man at the end of ten. The fault will be his own if he fail. Nature has done everything for the Manitoba farmer that Nature can do for any farmer; and it rests with him to do the rest. div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

_ Tag Prresz.—The average number of pulsations in a healthy adult is from 70 to 75 in a minute ; but there are persons who when they are quite well have always a pulse of 80 or 90, and there are others in whom the pulse seldom rises above 60. The pulse rate varies considerably at differ- ent ages. The average number of beats in the minute is as follows :—At birth, 140; during infancy, 120 to 130; in childhood, 100; in youth, 90; in adult age, 75; in old age, 65 to 70. In decrepitude, it is said the pulse once more increases in frequencey. The rate of the pulse is usually quicker in the standing than in the sitting posture, and in the sitting than in the recumbent. It is faster in the female than in the male, by from six to fotrteen beats, but this difference is not noticeable in young children. It is quick- ened by exertion or excitement. It is quickened by meals, and while varying thus from time to time during the day is, on the whole, quicker in the evening than in the early morning. It is said to be, on the whole, quicker in summer than in winter. Even independently of muscular exertion, it is quickened by great altitudes. In disease the pulse may acquire a degree of frequency scarcely culable to the touch—a rate of from 150 to 200, being in some cases re- corded. A rapid pulse, if strong, full, and hard, indicates inflammation or fever; but if small and very rapid, it points to a state of great debility, such as is often present in the last stage of typhoid and other fevers. On tbe other hand, in apoplexy sometimes, or when fainting is impending, or in certain affections of the heart, the pulse may be very slow. —The Family Physician. GALILEO'S ANAORADL—It had been objected to the theory of Copernicus, which made Venus an interior planet—one, that is, revolving between the Earth arid the Sun—that in this case it should show phases like the moon's, and,accord- ing to somewhat uncertain tradition, Copernicus replied that such was in fact the case, and that these changes would one day be distinguished. However this may be, it is certain that one of the earliest revelations of the telescope in the hands of Galileo was, that Venus did pass, like the Moon, from a slender crescent when near the Sun, to fuller round. ness as it withdrew from it. When this most interesting fact was discovered by him, ,he was divided between the wish to withhold the news of it till he could make more complete observations, and the fear that if he kept eilence some one else might anticipate him in the announcement. In our days a scientific man, under such circumstances, would probably write the history of his discodery, and de- posit it, under seal, in the custody of some learned society, so that he might establieh his priority if it were afterwards questioned. Galileo solved his dilemma by another means then in use, but which he employed with uncommon in- g.enuity. There is a familiar game which consists in taking the letters which form some common word, and giving them, jumbled into disorder, to an opponent, who is to arrange them, if he can, to re-spell the word which they compose. Galileo first briefly wrote his discovery in the words, "Cynthiec jiguras amulatur Mater Amorum," or (freely rendered) " Venus imitates the phases of the moon." lie might have simply printed, in irregular order, the let- ters which compose the above sentence, with tolerable con- fidence that no one but himself could re-compose them into their true meaning; but he did more, and himself re-com- posed them into still another sentence, " Hoc immatura a ' me jam frustra leguntur, 0p.," or "Things unripe for dis- closure, read in vain by others, are read by me," which thus both contained an announcement of a withheld die. covery, and a taunt to those who were challenged to read his riddle. Anyone who will be at the pains to devise a similar anagram will perhaps be of the opinion that the work is as difficult as the original observation it embodies, if not as meritorious. However this may be, the device served its purpose, and no one has ever disputed Galileo's claim to the discovery. After he saw fit to make it known, other and improved telescopes were directed to Venus, and it was found that the planet was a globe presenting spots on its surface, and by these it was discovered to revolve, like the Earth, in a little less than 24 hours.—Science for AU.

A POET'S GIFT.—A pleasant incident in the life of Oliver Wendell Holmes is related. At a country fair for charity, the ever-popular post-office was sadly in need of letters, when a lady, discovering the witty poet among the audience, requested him to furnish an epistle for the occasion. Quick as thought, he took a sheet of paper, and between its folds placed a $1 bank note; turning to the first page, he wrote the following : Dear lady, whoso'er thou art, Turn this poor page with trembling care; But hush, oh hush thy 'beating heart, The one thou lov'st best will be there. In obedience to the poet's injunction, the page turned dis- closed the attractive greenback of the value of $l, and to prove the truth of his assertion he made the following ap- peal on the opposite page from the bank deposit— Pair lady, lift thine eyes and tell . If this is not a truthful letter, This lathe one thou lovest And naught (0) would make thee love it better. A LANCASTRIAN'S VISIT TO PETTICOAT LANE.—Amongst the trippers to London on thelast Bank Holiday were a few sparks from Lancashire. One of them, who has always esti- mated hirelf as a knowing man, thought he would convince his companions that he actually was one; so he took them to that far-famed mart known as Petticoat-lane. After looking around for some time he espied a nice suit of clothes hanging at a stall presided over by a young Jewess. Think- ing the clothes would suit him, he began bantering the young lady down in the price, and after considerable hag- gling he finally became the purchaser for the small sum of eighteenpence. He threw down the money, and was about to walk away when the young lady, with the blandest of smiles, stopped him, and said, "You veel pe going py te train; so veel you allow me to wrap your parcel up," at the same time taking hold of the clothes. Our verdant friend was so bewitched by her manners that he allowed her to have all her own way, and stood gazing upon her Hebrew features instead of watching her hands. She by some dexterous movement or sleight-of-hand trick, folded up a parcel and gave it to him, and in the most obsequious manner possible bowed him away from the stall. He walked off as proud as Lucifer, and chuckled to his friends over the cheap bargain he bad made. He also took extra care of his parcel until he got back to Lancaster. On his arrival borne he was in hot haste to show his friends the valuable treasures he had brought from the great city, and amongst other things he with great ceremony unloosed his Petticoat-lane "prize," when to his great consternation out fell an old nail bag not worth a farthing, and his snit of clothes had vanished." TLIE IRISH LAND ACT. The Irish Land Commissioners have issued i statement of the benefits conferred by the Land Act (Ireland), 1881, upon the Irish tenant farmers. These benefits are thus briefly described:—

Fair Rent: Every existing tenant from year to year in Ireland of an ordinary agricultural or pastoral holditg is entitled to have a fair rent fixed for his holding, either by the County court Judge or by the Land Commission' or it may be settled by agreement with the landlord, or by ar- bitration.

Security of Tenure.—Whenever a fair rent is fixed, either by the Court or Commision, or by agreement, or by arbitra- tion, the rent cannot be raised or altered for fifteen years, nor can the tenant be disturbed during that period. In the last year of the fifteen years the tenant can again get the rent settled and a new term of fifteen years granted, and so on. It is not, therefore, merely a term of fifteen years which the tenant gets, but practically a term renewable every fifteen years. It amounts to this, that the tenant paying a fair rent and treating the land in a proper tenantable way, and not subdividing or subletting his farm, will be safe from eviction or arbitrary increase of rent, and his rent cannot be I increased by reason of his own improvements. Sale of tenancies.—Every tenant may sell his tenancy to one person at the best price he can get, but the landlord is to have first the right of buying, at a price either agreed on between the parties or to be fixed by the cond. Acquisition of the Holding Out-and-Out by the Tenant. ' —There are provisions in the Act authorising the Land Commision to advance, money to tenauts to enable them to purchase their holdings and become absolute owners of them.

Fixed Leases.—There are also provisions enabling tenants for life and other limited owners to give leases in perpetual- Hy to tenants. The privileges conferred are then described in detail, under the headings, "Fair rent and security of tenure," "Arrears of rent," "Pending ejectments," "Leaseholders," "Unfair leases," "Judicial leases," "Fixed tenancies," "Labourers," "Acquisition of Land—peasant proprietors," "Emigration." Upon all these points the clauses of the bill are explained in language easily understood. The summary concludes:— • The above are some of the great advantages conferred on Irish tenant farmers by the Lahti Act (Ireland) 1881, which provides for all Security in their holdings the fixing of fair rents, and the right of free sale; and affords the opportunity to occupiers to become the owners in fee of their holdings. It is not intended by the foregoing statement to set forth or include all the provisions of the Act, but only to afford a general view of its more important provisions. Any person requiring information can apply (by letter) to the Secretary, Land Commission, 24 Upper Merion-street, Dublin.

MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT AND THEIR *VOTES. During the prolonged session of Parliament just con- cluded there were no fewer than 411 divisions in the House of Commons, of which 259 took place before, and 152 after, midnight. The highest number of members taking part in • any one division was 556, on March 25, on the question of the withdrawal of the British troops from Afghanistan, and it is remarkable that this is exactly the same number as were present at the most numerously attended division last year. On the 9th of August 438 members entered the division lobbies, a larger number than ever probably previously seen Within the walls of the House so late in the session. There were only three divisions at which more than 500 members were present, viz., on March 14 (urgency for supply), on March 25 (Afghanistan), and on May 19 (Lord Eleho's motion on the Irish Land Law Bill). On three occasions the "No " lobby had only a single occupant. Calculating that each division occupied only 15 minutes, the time con- sumed by honourable members in walking through the lobbies amounted to over 11 &aye of time hours each. Out of 411 divisions, there were 266 on questions upon or arising out of the Irish difficulty, viz., 87 on the Coercion Bill, 53 on the Arms Bill, and 126 on the Land Law Bill. The total number of voles recorded during the session was 100,113, or an average of 244 for each division, and an average of 156 to each of the 640 members of which the House is at present constituted. Of these 100,000 votes, 71,506 were given by Liberal member, 27,560 by Conservatives, and 11,047 by Home Rulers. On the 9th of March there were 14 divisions, and on this one night 4,087 votes were recorded. The credit of having taken part in the greatest number of divisions rests with the two junior Government whips, Mr. Cotes, and Sir A. D. Hayter, who voted 407 and 406 times respectively. The next highest is Mr. Warton with 405 votes; and then come the two senior Government whips, Lord Richard Gros- venor with 404, and Lord Kensington with 387 votes; close upon the latter comes Mr. W. M. Johnson (Solicitor General for Ireland), with 384 votes. There were three members of the House who never voted at all. The Premier voted 254, the Leader of the Opposition 202, and Mr. Parnell 197 times, while the Conservative whips (Mr. Rowland Winn and Lord Crichton) toos part respectively in 225 and 183, and Major Nolan (the Home Rule whip).in 306 divisions. A compari- son with the 1880 session of the present Parliament shows that though the House sat a greater number of hours after midnight this year than in any previous session since the passing of the Reform Bill in 1832, the proportion of divi- sions taken after twelve o'clock is less by nearly 5 per cent than last year. THE CONDITION Or PRESIDENT GARFIELD.— REMOVAL TO LONGBRANCH. President Garfield's surgeons had a consultation on Satur- day, at which it was decided to remove the patient to Long Branch as soon as possible. WASHINGTON, Tuesday.—President Garfield passed a good night, awl at 6-15 arrived at the railway station, where he was placed in a combination carriage, and the train for Longbranch. The President seemed to enjoy the ride. thellkioriTnitonz, Tueslay.—The President stood the fatigue of roeY with rerdarkable fortitude. NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.

At the monthly meeting held on Monday, Mr. Gooch pre- sided. There were also present Col. McCorqsodale, Mesers. Fairclough, Forster, Pardey, Winstanley, Worsley (law clerk), and Brierley (surveyor). THE COMMITTEES. _ _

At a meeting of the Finance Committee on the 10th ult., accounts amounting to £443 9s. 44. were examined and signed for payment. Mr. George Wood was re-elected chair- man of the committee for the ensuing year.—At a meeting of the School Attendance Committee, held on the 15th ult., Mr. Ball, the school attendance officer, reported that for the quarter ending Jane, 1881, there were 2,175 children on the books, in average attendance 1,579; as compared with 2,133 and 1,473 respectively for the March quarter of 1881. Mr. Birley was re-elected chairman of the committee.—The Gas and Water Committee, at their meeting held on the 15th August, re-elected Mr. Winstanley as chairman. The Sur- veyor reported that the water had been turned off the town by the railway company at Earlestown on the 4th and sth, in consequence of their pumping engine at Parkside break- ing down. Mr. Brierley was instructed to write to Mr. Webb, again calling his attention to the necessity of at once providing duplicate apparatus at Parkside, as suggested in the letter to him on the sth July, 1878 The testing appara- tus being now fixed at the gas works, it was ordered that the fees for the testing and removidg of meters be as follows :- 2 or Slight meter, 25.; 5 light, 2s. 6d.; 10 light, 3s. t3d.; 20 light, 5e.; and for any size above 20 light, 1034 the money to be paid in advance.—The Highway, Public Works and Sanitary Committee held a meeting on the 15th ult., when Mr. W. Pennington was re-elected chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. Turner, of Manchester, attended, and explained the advantages of his new dividable pail closet over any other system of dealing with the excreta of towns, and the committee promised to give the matter consideration. The Surveyor drew the attention of the committee to the appar- ent impracticability of the railway company providing accees for carts to the Earlestown goods station from Alma- street consequent upon the alterations made in their sidings, and advised that the paving, dzc., of Suez•street and Alma- street be proceeded with. It was decided that the Surveyor confer with the Law-Clerk, and, if necessary, see Mr. Worth- ington, the company's engineer, respecting the new gateway and other accommodation. The board room was recom- mended to be re-papered and painted. Plans for the erection of two cottages at Newton Common by Mr. William Smith were submitted and approved. The minutes were confirmed. In reply to the Chairman, the Surveyor said Mr. Worthing- ton was away from home 'and nothing had been done in regard to the gateway at Earlestown. The minutes were confirmed. The Clerk read a letter from the Local Govern- ment Board confirming the appointment of Dr. Watkins, as medical officer, at a salary of £5O per annum.

• THE BOARD AND BANE HOLIDAYS. Mr. PARDEY, in the absence of Mr. Pennington, who had given notice of motion, moved that the resolution passed on the 2nd July, 1877, which stated that the next monthly meeting occurring upon Bank Holiday be held on the day following. Tuesday, the 11th August, be rescinded, and that the first Monday in August be the date of meeting.— After some discussion, in which it was pointed ont that the motion would only apply to the August Bank Holiday, Mr. Pardey amended his resolution as follows: "That the resolution of July, 1877, be rescinded, and that Bank Holi- days be not observed unless previously arranged."—Colonel MCCORQUODALE seconded the motion, which was carried.

INFECTIOUS DISEASES AND ISOLATION. Mr. WiNSTANLEY wished to ask a question about the In- fectious Diseases Hospital: He had been told, though he could not vouch for its truth, that the Hospital was full and not able to take any patients; and a case came before the Board of Guardians at Newton 'on Thursday, front which it appeared that a member of a certain family at Earlestown was seized with an infectious disease. A private doctor was employed, and the attention of the Medial Officer of Health was not called to the case. The result was that the disease spread to the other members of the family for want of isolation. One of them died, and about ten days afterwards the head of the family was taken ill. The whole of the family would now have to be main- tained out of the public rates. The reason assigned for the non-removal of the family was that the relieving officer said there was no room in the hospital. If that was so it was important that the Board should see that proper means were provided in the town for, the purpose of effecting isolation. —Mr. PARDEE : Was the application to relieving officer?— Mr. WINSTANLET : Yes.—Mr. Palmas: Doe! the relieving officer say there is no room 7-Mr. WINSTANLII : Dr. Watkins gives answer that there is no room.—The Cuatnmarr :It is a question for the Board of Guardians.—Mr. WINSTANLEY : It is a question for you.—The Cattatate said they had made provision for these cases, but no application had been made to take this case in.—Colonel MCCORQUODALE re- markedai that the Hospital had to receive the patients if they ( room; if not they would make some arrangement.—Mr. to deal Yw i saidth t me aatpteprl.i—camtiorn. wwieNnss „Nthrough the relieving officer, and the Board of Guardian were the proper persons cation was made to the Medical Officer of Hseaaidltht,hweha lat- tended to the case, and finding certain things required for the subsistence of the family, gave an order to the relieving officer for beef and milk. He wished to draw their attention to the fact that no proper means of isolation having been provided in this case it had been disastrous and might lead to furthbr loss of life.—Mr. PAIIDET : I understood you to say that it did not come before our medical officer until one death had occurred.—Mr. WINSTANLET said it was in the hands of a private doctor. It was for their consideratin when they could not make some arran,ement with the medical gentleman to give notice to the Lard when called in to an infectious disease.—Mr. PARDEY: We have already done tbat.—Mr. WINSTANLEY : They have not done so.—The SURVEYOR : They have been written to.—The CHAIRMAN observed that everything had been done by the Beard that they could do, and they could deal with the cafes when they came properly before them—Mr. IVINSTANLEy : Not for isolation.—The CHAIRMAN: There has not been an appli- cation made to our surveyor.—Mr. WINSTANLEY said the inspector and the medical officer were there—Mr. PARDEy : Before you went there, Mr. Brierley, had the relieving officer appeared in the matter P—The SURVEYOR: I think not, sir. He said Mr. Winstanley wanted the healthy per- sons removing before they contracted the disease.—Mr. PARDEY : That is beyond our province.—Some further con- versation took place, after which Colonel McCoacuoneva said if the medical officer had refused to send a patient because there was no room, then it was his duty to have brought it before the Board.—The CHAIRMAN: Certainly.— Mr. PARDEy moved that the matter be referred to the Sani- tary Committee to ask for an explanation from Dr. Watkins. —Mr. FAIRCLOUGH seconded the motion which was carried. —The Cratna said he would make Inquiries at Warrington as to the state of the Infectious Diseases Hospital and com- municate with the surveyor. STATION ACCOMMODATION AT EARLESTON. The CHAIRMAN said he had been asked to bring forward the desirability of asking the committee to provide a better station on the curve at Earlestown.—Mr. WINSTANLEY : They are doing so.—The CHAIRMAN: When did they com- mence doing it ?—Mr. WINSTANLEY thought they were putting up a shed, and a better than the present one.—The CHAIRMAN said it might be in contemplation, but the company had done nothing yet.—The SURVEYOR said some time ago he wrote to Mr. Shaw complaining of the accommo- tion, and three months ago he received an answer stating in- structions had been given for something to be done.—The CHAIRmAN hoped they would get a more comfortable station for the winter.—The meeting then terminated.

"The thaemcohn'-' elusion of the service, which lasted about three ceremony of kissing the hands of the newly-ordained Priests. was gone through by the community, their example beingtr. followed by the whole of the congregation. In the afe noon a second service was held, at which there was again a very large attendance. The Rev. Father Haza de Radlitz delivered an eloquent address on "The Catholic priesthood," in which he pointed out the dignity and obligations of the sacred ministry. The Bishop subsequently gave solemn Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament. '[he brief history of the German Jesuits at Ditton Hall is one of much interest. When they were expelled the Fatherland, in 1871, a large number came to England, and the Hall was presented to them as a refuge by Lady Bretherton Stapleton, who added to her generous gift by building St. Michael's at a cost of between £20,000 and £30,000. The offertories on Sunday will be applied towards defraying the coat of a new pulpit. The priests and ecclesiastics at the college devote them- selves almost exclusively to the study of theology. The Rev. Father Stentrup, who has been five years rector, is about to leave for Exarten, in Holland, and his place will be taken by the Rev. Father Hoevel, formerly provincial of the German province of the order. The names of the newly- ordained priests are as follow :—Andrew Walsh Antony Bruder, Charles Schlitz, Francis Borscht, Frederick Evers, William Plenkers, Henry Klene, Ferdinand Schwick, Herman Haug, Joseph Haan, Joseph de Lassberg, Matthias Reich- mann, Theophilus Nyssen, Thomas Bruhl, Aloisius Bosch, and Francis Fechteler. They will not immediately leave the college to join any mission, but will continue their studies for a year or twe longer. At the close of that period, some will be sent into different parts of the world, as many priests of the Society of Jesus have already been sent since 1872 from Ditton Hall to North America, Brazil, Africa, and Asia. Others may stay in England, or be stationed in various countries in the continent.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 10, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 10, 1881.
OPENING OF ST._ PAUL'S CHURCH.
ST. HELENS.

The growing need of church accommodation in the parish of St. Thomas, St. Helens, was so apparent 12 months ago that the Vicar, the Rev. J. C. Pigot, and his officers, began to seriously consider how it must be provided. One church was clearly not sufficient to minister to the spiritual neces- sities of a population of 10,000, and which was rapidly in- creasing. Besides, by far the greater proportion of that number were working people, who could not afford to pay pew rents, and who, in consequence, probably stayed away altogether from the fear of intruding on other seat holders. A mission church, where there was no such fear, but where all would be made welcome, was therefore thought the most feasible plan. There are also always, a certain number averse to making any exertion to attend church, and a mission church would be the best means of bringing those I within "the fold." In November, 1880, a committee, with the Vicar, the Rev. J. C. Pigot, as chairman, and Mr. W. R. Ward, as hon. sec., was formed to take the matter in hand. The other members were the curate, the Rev. T. S. Jagg, and Messrs. Baddeley, Norman, Edmondson, Fishwick, Beckett, Mather, Varley, Oscar, W. Owen, Foreman, and F. Hodgson. All anxiety as to the site for the proposed erec- tion was quickly set at rest by the Vicar's family giving a piece of ground at the upper part of Napier-street; and as early as possible in this year building operations were com- menced by Mr. Lawrensen, builder, Kirkland-street, from designs by Mr. Gandy, architect, Hall-street. On Wednes- day last the opening service was held. The building is of brick, relieved from absolute plainness on the outside by buttresses which are placed at regular intervals around it. The inside, though not possessing any elegant furniture, or speciality in design, is made particularly pleasing by the arrangement of the rafters, which are of stained pitch pine. That wood is also used for the forms, which have reversible backs. In the left hand corner of the upper end of the building is the vestry, and on the right the organ chamber, at present occupied by a small American organ. Between these is the communion, on the table of which Is a hand- some communion cloth, the gift of Mrs. McMochatta, the widow of the late vicar. It is of dark crimson, and worked in black and gold. The building is exceedingly well lighted and ventilated, and has been erected, including the furoiture, at a cost of £1,400. It is estimated to seat 400 persons. Nearly £5OO has been raised by voluntary subscriptions, and the rest is expected to be obtained by a Swiss cottage bazaar to be held next November. The efforts of the church, how- ever, do not end with this building. On the left is a large plot of land generously given to the mission by the vicar's family, and intended at some future date to be the site of a handsome church. When that thne arrives, the present building will be converted into a school. The parishioners must feel extremely grateful to the vicar and his family for their open-handed generosity and zeal in the cause of religion. The following clergy were present at the opening services :—Revs. S. Wilkinson, vicar, St. Paul's, Warring- ton; R. R. Moore, vicar, Ravenhead ; E. St. A. Duke, curate, St. Paul's, Warrington; W. Smith, of Manchester; S. A. Spooner, B. S. Clarke, T. B. M•Lean, Ormskirk; J. Brame, secretary Additional Curates' Society; J. Barnacle, J. C. Pigot, vicar, and T. S. Jagg, curate. There was a large con- gregation. After a hymn had been sang, the vicar read the license for the church, which had been granted by the Bishop of Liverpool. The vicar conducted the first part of the service, and the Rev. T. S. Jaggp the carate, the second part. The first lesson was read by the Rev. J. Barnacle, and the second by the Rev. J. Brame. Miss Pigot presided at the organ. The Rev. Canon Barclay, of Runcorn, had been announced to preach the sermon, but he was unable to be present, and the Rev. S. Wilkinson, vicar of St. Paul's, War- rington, took his place. He selected for his text the Ist versa of the 35th chapter Isaiah, "The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice and blossom as the rose." He said he felt a solemn pleasure in being the first to unfurl the banner of Christ's cross in that place, and to point the sinful to Jesus Christ, " the lamb of God who taketh away the sins of the world." It was also pleasing to him as the Church bore the sameename as the Church in which be ministered and in which their vicar had laboured some time. In the Old Testament they saw Oh influence of Christ's work con- stantly foretold. By His coming the desert should be filled with flowers and beautiful gardens, in place of darkness. , Before He came the law was an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. Now it was "Love your enemies, do good to them that hate you, and pray, for those that despitefully use you." What had been the effect of His coming on our own beloved country of England ? There was once a time when England was a land of desolations when human sac- rifices were offered to false gods, when cruelty was con- tinually raging, and when man died without hope, when the friend who stood at the bedside could not point out to the poor sufferer any hope of immortality as they could now to their friends. But by God's providence Christian mis- sionaries came on this war ground and taught the inhabi- tants better things—never to sacrifice fellow beings to false gods, and to keep peace as subjects of the Prince of Peace, and to do good to others while they lived, so that when they came to die they might look forward to fulfilling the hope of a world beyond the grave where there would be no more sorrow, pain, suffering, or death. There were many, doubt- less, who had learned to serve God in the parish Church of St. Thomas. But surely one church was not sufficient for a population of 12,00, and their good vicar determined to make an effort. And it had been a great effort to him; it had cost him much money, self-denial, and many an anxious thought. He bad with his :noble coadjutors finished the work, and they were met that day to dedicate that house to the worship of our. Father in Heaven. That Church had been built for a noble purpose. There the poor penitent might go and confess his sins to God. There too they would bring their children, and dedicate them to the service of that Saviour they loved so well, for Christ said "Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not for of such is the King- dom of Heaven." He asked them all to make use of that "house of prayer," and they would find it indeed to be a very gift of God. In erecting that church their vicar had done his duty and they must do theirs by attending and sup- porting it. 'lt was impossible to estimate what good would be done by their example and influence upon others. Many helpers would be required, but he was sure that the vicar's appeal would be respmded to by all. The services that day, had been very encouraging; so many being present proved that they appreciated the work and were heartily anxious that it should succeed. Let him add one word of caution. There was an old saying that "You must not rob Peter to pay Paul," and in that parish they must not rob St. Thomas to pay St. Paul. The church had been built for the addi- tional population of the parish which could not find room in St. Thomas's church. Therefore, while doing all they could to further the work in that part of the parish, they must not forget the old Parish church. He knew there was a certain amount of danger in having a new place in a parish. He trusted the services which had been commenced in that church would spiritually enrich the people of that neighbourhood. After speaking of the necessity for indi- vidual effort, he said he hoped that the work so auspiciously commenced might be done in God's name and go on and prosper, that many souls might be saved, and God grant that all of them who had met in St. Paul's at the opening services and joined in God's praises, may arrive at that happy home for which these services were meant to prepare them.

div.head: OPENING OF SOUTHPORT NET MARKETS.
div.p: OPENING OF SOUTHPORT NET MARKETS.
LORD DERBY ON THE PROSPERITY OF THE
COUNTRY.

At Southport, on Wednesday, Lords Derby and Lathom opened the new public markets and promenade, in the presence of a large number of spectators, including the mayors of the neighbouring boroughs and several members of Parliament, amongst the latter being the Hon. F. A. Stanley, M.P., Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., and Mr. W. E. Briggs, M.P. The new market is an exceedingly large and handsome structure, and has been erected at a cost of £25,000. An extension of the promenade has involved a cost ef £40,000. The effect of the extension has been to re- claim no less than 48 acres of building land from the sea. The promenade is now a mile and a half long.ln the after- noon the Mayor entertained Lords Derby and Lathom, Col, I Stanley, M.P., the High Sheriff of Lancashire, Mr. W. E. I Briggs, M.P., Mr. J. G. McMinnies, NLP., Major Gerard, the Mayors of Accrington, Bury, St. Helens, Barrow, Bootle, Huddersfield, Oldham, Chester, Wigan, and Leeds, and others, at a banquet in the Cambridge Hall. Lord Derby, in his address, spoke of the progress of British trade within I the past decade. He said that on this matter we ought to look at a decade. It would be found that between 1871 and I 1881, the material prosperity of the, codntry had increased to a considerable extent. Our imports had, increased from £303,000,000 to £411,000,000; our exports in 1871 were £244,000,000, and in 1881 they had risen to £276,000,000. The number of paupers 11 years ago was 1,079,000, but last year the number dropped to 837,000. The income tax returns showed that in two years tax had been paid on an increase of 133,000,000 of money. The nation, he re- marked, was like a strong man assailed with a slight sick- ness, who had some apprehension of death, but from whom the malady passed in a few weeks, and he then found him- self as strong as ever.

SCOTCH FARMERS AND TIIE PRIME MINISTEM—A meeting of Aberdeenshire farmers has been held to take steps to present Mr. Gladstone, on the occasion of his visit to the North in the autumn, with a token of recognition of his past services to the interests of agriculture.—Mr. Bruce Fornet presided, and spoke of Mt. Gladstone's extraordinary services in connection with the passing of the Irish Land• Act. He declared that if Ireland had got three F's Scotland wanted five F's, and that the farmers should never cease agitating till there was free trade in land, which was given by the Almighty for the benefit of all and not for the exclusive patrimonial possession of a few --It was resolved to present Mr. Gladstone with an illuminated address on the occasion of his proposed visit to Haddo House, the cost to be defrayed by penny subscriptions throughout the country.
