div.head: ENGLISH CHURCH UNION.
div.p: ENGLISH CHURCH UNION.

ANNUAL MEETING OF WARRINGTON BRANCH. The Rev. Canon Heron, vice-chairma,n, yresided at the ,annual meeting of the Warrington Branch of the English Church Union, on Monday afternoon, in the Masonic Rooms, Sankey-street. There was a fair attcndance, and amongst those present were Rev. Halcot Ash, of Arley; Rev. C. J. Winger, High Legh ; Messrs. J. Tinsley, P. Pearse, J. White, H. Houghton, J. Bolton, Acton, Looker, W. John- son, oh.

The SuctutTAßY (Mr. John White) read the following letter from Mr. R. E. Egerton Warburton, chairman : "Arley Hall, Northwich, Sept. 3, 1881.—Dear Sir,—You will not have expected my attendance at the meeting of the Warrington Branch a the English Church Union, of which I have received notice. At the same time, as nominal chairman, it would he ungracious in me not to convey to you my regret at my inability to be present to assure the meeting that I cordially agree with their object in its sym- pathy with Mr. Green and to express my abhorrence of the intolerance of which he is the victim. However painful it is to think that he should be singled out for persecution for opinions which so many hold, and for which so many would be willing to share his imprisonment, we must not the leas feel grateful for the courage and endurance by which he has induced the public to give the subject a thought, and we may hope that the correspondence which has been the re- sult, especially the letters that have appeared in the Mors- ing Post, may open the eyes of those at least who are without prejudice, to what is the real grievance of which we complain, and to make them clearly comprehend the rights for which we are contending." The SECRETARY said when the Rev. S. F. Green was im- prisoned it was inconvenient to hold a meeting, so he took upon himself to write to Mr. Green, in the name of the Branch, to express their sympathy with him, and he had re- ceived from him the following letter :—" Lancaster, April, 1881.—My dear Mr. White,—l am most grateful to you for your very kind and cheerful letter. I think you make more of my very ordinary effort to maintain the rights and liberties of the Church than it at all deserves; and I am quite sure there are hundreds, who, if similarly situated, would do precisely the same. I certainly hope that the next priest called upon will be spared the outrage of bailiffs in his house for 14 weeks, for in civilized warfare women and children are usually respected, and it was a great dis- tress to me to be brought away here leaving my poor wife and her little children in such a state of anxiety, and having to leave the house, and hearing from time to time of the insolence she had to put up with when compelled occasionally to go home. That is over, at any rate pro tern, and I am Indeed thankful. Everyone here is very kind, and I fear I may reconcile my- self to a prolonged stay, as I see that my friends entirely failed to make out a case for me on technical grounds. But Ido not doubt but that this is for the best. We have tried throughout, under a good deal of provocation, to carry on this contest on the highest principles, and I am quite sure that our Divine Master will continne to use us to His glory so long as we strive to walk and war in His spirit."

• - The CHAIRMAN, after remarking that it was unnecessary for him to remind them of the objects of the Union, said it might perhaps be right and proper to state that whatever its objects were! such they still continued to be, and that they were subjected to unremitting persecution at the hands of that part of the Puritan section of the Church of England which, through an organisation called the Church Associa- tion, did not cease to persecute to the utmost of its power clergy,a,m agreeing with them in the main essentiala of Christianity but differing from them in some of their views upon comparatively minor points. It was much to be re- gretted that this warfare should still be carried on. He was quite sure they all desired peace—peace within the borders of the Church of England, was, he was sure, the wish and the aim and the prayer of every member of the Church Union. If such a state of things could not be brought about, the fault, he thought, did not lie with them, for their position was simply one of defence; but the fault of the continuance of this state of dissention was surely traceable to, and to be laid at the door of, the Church Association, which continued with unabated vigour to carry out its cruel persecution of those who differed from them. If a time of peace was to be restored to the Church, as it appeared to him it could only be through circumstances such as the following :—First of all, if their opponents desired content- ment and peace they must renounce their aggressive course of conduct towards them and others who agreed with them, and they must be content to live and let live. They knew 'that at the present time all the members on their side of the question were perfectly willing that no effort should be made to expel members of the Puritan part of the Church from the communion of the Church of England. They made no charges against them. They took no active part in promoting anything like legal proceedings; bat the whole of those things proceeded from the other side, and until they arrived at the conviction that it is both wrong, unscriptural, and impolitic to persecute people for their conscientious opinions, he for one could see no prospect of a period of peace for the Church of England. It might come, with God's blessfhg, sooner than he looked for It; he hoped it might. Secondly :—lf there was to be peace, he thought there must be a revision of some of the recent judgments that have taken place. Undoubtedly those judgments have been passed from a want of information—he would not use the word ignorance in respect to the highly respectable lawyers who had given those judgments, but they certainly were not experts in the matters brought before them, and probably with very upright and good intentions they bad passed judgments which further consideration might, be hoped, lead them to modify if not to rescind. Further, he thought there must be, should he say, a repeal of the Public Worship Regulation Act. That he could hardly hope for, but if they could get a recognition of the rights of the Church which had been secured to her by charters of early date, and a modification or adaptation of that Act to the relative positions of Church and State, he would then have some hope that they might have peace and comfort within their borders. Those two thipgs seemed to him to be essential to the restoration of anything like a state of comfort within their communion. There was one bright feature of the present time, and that was the appointment of a commission of enquiry into the administration of ecclesiastical law, and he hoped they would be able to hit upon some scheme by which the ill effects that have arisen from the Public Worship Regulation Act might be modified and in part removed. Adverting to the general state of the Union, he said it was a very great satisfaction to be able to state that in spite of the obloquy with which those high in ecclesiastical position had sought to bespatter their association, in spite of the hard speeches they had made from time to time the number of members had greatly increased during the past year and afforded a very decided proof of the increased anxiety that it met with in various parts of the kingdom. Of their own branch he was afraid he could not speak with quite so much gratification. They had cer- tainly no considerable increase if they had any increase at all. He then adverted to the CB9O of the Rev. S. F. Green, who, he said, was a successful minister of the Gospel, a clergyman who had gained an influence over a class of the community that very few clergymen bad been able to accomplish, a man who at oo high in the reputation of his private character, and had received the good word even of his persecuting diocesan. (Applause.) They all knew that, bat a they sufficiently consider the hardships to which he individually was subject? There was the degradation of imprisonment, and that in a high spirited man, with a clear conscience in what he was doing must indeed be painful in the extreme. They knew he had not only been carried away from his contented congregation, but deprived of the society., to a very large extent, of his wife and fantly, but they did nob know, and they never could know unless they were in the same circumstances, the wearisomeness which must have come over him after upwards of five months'con- finement in a solitary room. Mr. Green was stubborn, and they were very glad—(applause)—for if he were to give way it would be a real blow to the principles of the Church of England. They hoped God would maintain him in his firmness as long as it might be requisite. (Applause.) The point for them to dTell upon was the fact that he was imprisoned for the maintenance of a principle in which every member of the Church of England was deeply interested. He was a confessor for the maintenance of the rights of the Church as a branch of the constitution of England as it at present stood, but mere than that, he was a confessor for the prin- ciple which maintained the spiritual rights of the Church for the self-government of herself subject to the supremacy of the Queen in all spiritual matters. If the class'which put Mr. Green into prison were to gain the day, and to pre- vail, there would be nothing before the Church of England but complete subjection to the civil power of the State. They knew what would be the end of that. They knew the calamity it would bring upon them both spiritually and temperally, and therefore be thought they were bound to feel the deepest gratitude to Mr. Green for the conscientious perseverance with which be maintained the rights of the Union to which they belonged. (Applause.)

div.head: SECRETARY.S REPORT.
div.p: SECRETARY.S REPORT.

The Secretary's report stated: "Though no general meet- ing of the branch has been held during the past year, the Union itself has been more than usually alive. Indeed, the year has been one of great anxiety, and persecution has been carried to a point never before witnessed in this generation. Since September in last year, three faithful and devoted priets of the Church of England have been cast into prison, and though two have been released on technical grounds, a third, the Rev. S. F. Green, still remains in gaol, with every prospect of a lengthened imprisonment. It will be in the recollection of members that Mr. Green was present at our last annual meeting, and then gave us to understand that he was prepared to suffer his goods to be spoiled and his liberty to be taken away rather than to sur- render to Cresar the things which are God's, or to violate the vows of his ordination. We, as churchmen, are under a deep debt of gratitude to Mr. Green for the noble stand and sacrifice he is now making for the Church, and the members will this evening be asked to join in an expression of sym- pathy with, and thanks to, him. As a proof that the prin- ciples of the Union are rapidly increasing in public favour, it may be mentioned that at the last annual commemora- tion of the Union in June there were celebrations of the holy communion on behalf of the Union at no less than 91 churches in London and the immediate neighbourhood. The annual report showed that during the Year there had been a nett gain of nearly 2 000 members (all, of course, communicants), and that the total number of members and. associates was now nearly 20,000. The number now at- tached to the Warrington Branch is 60 as against 0 last year." The TRFASURFR (Mr. J. Bolters) read the statement of accounts, which showed a balance in hand of £1 2s.

The report and statement of accounts were adopted on the motion of Mr. TINSLEY, seconded by the Ref. C. J. WINSEEL The chairman, vice-chairman, secretary, treasurer, and the committee, consisting of .the Rev. E. D. Garvin, Rev. F. Slat:r, Mr. John Tinsley, and Mr. H. N. Houghton were re-elected. Rev. H. Asa moved "that thie meetiqg of the Warrington Branch of the English Church Union desires to express its deep sympathy with the Rev. S. F. Green in his imprison- ment, and it hearty thanks to him for the noble stand he is making against the unconstitutional interference of the secular powers in the spiritual affairs of the Chkrch." Mr. JOHN WHITE, in seconding the resolution, impressed upon them that Mr. Green was suffering for a great cause dear to all of them, and that they ought as far as lair in their power to do something to share the suffering with him. It was very hard to get people to take an interest in Church matters. A large number of people had no religion at all, and a great number were Dissenters, who were out of the question, and the Church people whenever they heard Mr Green's name mentioned said, "Oh, its Mr. Green the Ritualist; serve him right." That was as far as people in this neighbourhood had got, and it was necessary for them to repeat the story again and again, Mr. Green was in prison for contempt of a court sanctioned. by Parliament since Mr. Green's ordination. It was never intended by the constitu- tion of the Church that any court should be appointed by I the State alone, and that the Church should have no inter- ference. This court was appointed in direct opposition to the wishes of Convocation. Matters had got to such A pitch that even the lawyers themselves, he thought, did not know what ecclesiastical law was, and the fact remained, although Mr. Green was not imprisoned for contempt of court or breaking the law, it was felt necessary that a Royal Com- mission to enquire into the state of ecclesiastical law at the present time. The clerical members of the Church Asso- ciation were what they called Low Churchmen, and if they were such as he had seen in his lifetime, never a day passed but they broke the law themselves. The nominal complain- ante broke the law because they were not regular communi- cants of the Church of England, and the. Bishop was also a law breaker, as he was the person who permitted the trial to go on. If ever there was a case where the law needed not to be enforced this was the dase, and yet they found the Bishop of Manchester allowing it to go on. It had been one of the most disgraceful epochs in the history of this genera- tion, and no language that could be used was too strong to denounce it. (Applause). The resolution was carried, and a vote of thanks having been accorded to the chairman the meeting terminated. At the close petitions were signed praying for the release of the Rev. S. F. Green from prison.

div.head: GROSS CASE OF PARENTAL CRUELTY
div.p: GROSS CASE OF PARENTAL CRUELTY
AT PRESCOT.

• On Tuesday, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, Henry Sephton, Sewell-street, was charged with having, on the 2nd September, unlawfully and cruelly beaten his son, .James Sephton, eight years of age.—Superintendent Barker stated that on Friday defendant went to Liverpool, and during his absence the little boy allowed a bird to escape out of a cage. On returning and finding what the child had done, he be- came so aggravated that he a.:t to and thrashed the little I fellow most unmercifully with a strap. Information of the affair was given at the police station, and on Saturday Mr. Barker had the boy brought down. His right eye was much more discoloured than it was at the present time. There were contusions on the forehead, and on the side and back of the head. On seeing tilt, state of the boy, he took pro I ceedings against the father.—The boy corroborated this statement, and stated that while his father was thrashing him he turned round, and the strap caught him on the face, blackening his eye and injuring his fore- hoad.—Mr. Evans (to defendant) : You have beaten your I child unmercifully and cruelly.—Defendant : I was thrash- ing him on the back, and he turned round and the strap caught him on the eye. I was sorry as soon as I had done lit—Mr. Evans: It is beyond parental punishment.—Suglt. Barker: I had the boy examined by Dr. Morris, and I have a certificate from him as to the condition in which he found the boy.—Defendant, in answer to the Bench, said he had nothing to say, except that he was sorry.—Superinten- dent Barker said he laid the information against the defen- dant on public grounds.—Mr. Evan: Hare there been com- plaints P—Mr. Barker: I find that this man was summoned before the court in August, 1878, for assaulting this little boy, but the case fell through because there was no evidence except the mother's. He was summoned twice before that for assault. He ill-uses his wife and children very much.— Mr. Evans: It is a very bad 'case. It is a gross case of cruelty to treat so young a child so unmercifully no matter what offence it had committed. Its abominable. The de- fendant must pay a !fine of 40s. and costs, or one month's Imprisonment with hard labour.

PRESCOT lIIGTIWAY BOARD.

The monthly meeting of the above-named Board was held on Tuesday, at the clerk's offices, Derby-street, there being present Messrs. W. L. Evans, J.P. (chairman), Mr. Lowe (Rainhill), and 11. Fogg (Whiston), with Mr. H. Cross (clerk), and Mr. Wm. Goldsworth (surveyor).

THE BOARD SHORT OF MONEY. From a statement submitted by the clerk, it appeared that Knowsley owed £135, Rainhill £lOO, and Whiston £lOO in respect of the call made on the 12th April last; Bold had paid up. Nothing had been said since the last meeting, although the clerk had written to the overseers asking for immediate payment.—The CHAIRMAN said if the overseers would not pay the Board must make them.—Mr. LOWS thought it would be well to write to the overseers press- ing for payment, at once.—The CHAIRMAN said the clerk had already written.—Mr. FOGG observed that at Whiston they were in a predicament as to the collector. The superannuation of the old assistant overseer had not yet been confirmed, neither had the appointment of a deputy collector nor the appointment of a new assistant overseer which had lately been made, so that between the lot several of the ratepayers declined to pay their rates.—The CHAIR- MAN: Who are the overseers 7—Mr. FOGG : Mr. Hewitt and Mr. Smith.—The CHAIRMAN: They are responsible. They , must collect the rates themselves. The Board must have money or else we can't go on. We owe the bank £351, and there is an expenditure of £109; that makes £460 owing. If the overseers will not pay by urgent request, what shall we do ?—Mr. LOWS: Has the clerk threatened them with summonses 7—The CLERK: No.—The CHAIRMAN: He had no authority to do that. I think the best thing would be to instruct the clerk to inform them that proceedings would be taken unless the money was paid at once, or, at any rate, by a certain time.—Mr. Food: Suppose we give them a fortnight longer.—The CHAIRMAN: Give them ten days, so that Mr. Cross will have time to take out summonses for the next petty sessions if the money is not paid.—lt was accord- ingly resolved that the clerk write to the overseers of the townships in arrears informing them that he had instruc- tions to take proceedings if the money was not paid in ten days.—The Surveyor said the total amount of the new call was settled, and an arrangement had been made that one- half should be called for, for the half year ending March next. The call would be the same in amount as last year. The total amount for the half year was £1,285, classed as follows :—Bold £250, Rainhill £3OO, Knowsley £335, and Whiston £4oo.—lt was stated that the call would be pay- able in six weeks.—The Surveyor submitted his statement of expenditure for the five weeks ending September Ist, as follows :—Boldtlo Is. 3d., Knowsley £l2 ls.' Rainhill £3B 178. 11d., Whiston £l4 us., team labour £57 13s. 2P., new material £67 19s. sid., incidental expenses £8 4s. 7d., total £209 Bs. 5d., as compared with £262 14s. Id. in the preced- ing month.—Mr. FOGG asked when the Board would get the money from the county in respect of the roads.—The CHAIRMAN: Not for threo months. We got it on the Bth November last year. The accourts have not yet been audited.—Mr. Lowe observed that if the, new call was not paid at the expiration of next week they would be in the same position as at the present time.—Mr. Foci° remarked that they would be in a better position at the bank when the arrears were got in.

are dinning prophecies of evil omen into too receptive ears. Is there any real cause for this profound feeling of agitation ? Is British industry really on the wane ? Is our trade suffering from permanent depression ? Lord Derby gives a confident negative to these alarm- ist theories, and, what is more, substantiates his denial by figures which are beyond the reach of quibble or contradiction. He points out the excep- tional character of recent seasons. Much of the un- doubted agricultural depression has been due to the disastrous succession of rainy seed times and harvests. The farmers have had to fight against the irremedi- able conditions of nature, and this, coupled with the harsh terms of their tenure, has entirely exhausted many and impoverished more. But there is no reason te suppose that adverse meteorological influences are going to prevail for ever. There have been lean years in the world's history before now, and fat years have followed the lean ones. We may, therefore, reason- ably expect good seasons again. The special causes of the present depression will pass away, and the farmer will by and by have sunshine and fair weather in their season, and be able to multiply his produce and look cheerful once more. Lord Derby does not believe in the shutting out of English-grown produce from the market by the greater cheapness of foreign competition. There is an " insatiable" market close to the farmer's own doors, and he has nothing to fear from rivals 5,000 miles away. This comparative proximity to densely populated towns gives him an advantage which no amount of •coinpetition can interfere with in many articles of Production. Probably the present system of farm- ing will have to undergo some changes; most cer- tainly the land laws will have to bemodified in favour of the tenant; but, as long as ever the Atlantic sepa- rates England from America, the English farmer is in the superior position of having an " insatiable I market" of 35,000,000 people ready to take any I amount of produce he can supply. $o much for agri- culture. Lord Derby, in referring to the irrefutable evidence of figures with regard to trade, does not ! fall into the: mistake so common amongst amateur politicians of comparing one year with its immediate ! predecessors. Fluctuations of that kind are unre- liable. The only safe and satisfactery method is to compare decennial periods. Since 1870 our imports have increased from 303 millions per annum to 41 millions, and our exports from 244 millions to 286 millions. Thus even our export trade, about which there is so much lamentation, is vastly better' than ton years ago, the:average gain being more than four millions a year. The favourite theory of Fair Traders or Protectionists is that as our imports exceed our exports we are living upon our !capital. Lord Derby's reply to that is that oar foreign trade, especially our shipping, is enormously profitable, and that we have vast sums invested with foreign countries all over the world, from whom we are drawing tribute. If there is any truth in the theory that we are living upon our capital, there must be some evidence of it in those departments which may be regarded as the barometers of national prosperity. There cannot be a continual drain going on without certain indications of it. Lord Derby refers to savings banks, which are a sure index of the prosperity of the lower middle, and working classes, and he findsthatin 10 years the deposits have increased nearly one-half. Then, again, if a country is gradually being impoverished the records of pauperism will show it immediately. Ten years ago there were 0,079,000 paupers in England and Wales, whilst last year there were only 837,00o—a decrease of nearly a quarter of a million. The con- sumption of common popular luxuries, suoh as tea and sugar, has increased enormously; the returns of the income tax show that the trading classes are better off by 133 millions, and the population has rc• rearkably increased. Lord Derby pithily says with regard to these significant facts, "I should be apt to say that a nation so circumstanced was not in a bad way." No doubt we have had a check, but ici merely temporary, for every indication points to the steady and continual development of our resources. A return to good times is sure to come. The 1t trade returns issued have a healthy look, giving abundant ground for hopefulness. It suits the purpose of some people to take a gloomy view of the conditioik of this country and to propheorEngland's ultimate ruin. But the utter absurdity of the predictions and statemen, s of the Fair Traders is abundantly proved by the ! figures quoted by Lord Derby and the reputation he ! possesses for practical sagacity will, make his wise words influential among those who have been misled into believing that our trade is going to the dogs, and that the workingman will soon have no work to do.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY SEPTEMBER 10, 1881.

missioners the books belonging to the Institute, which number about 300, and the furniture and effects, at a valua- tion. Those who have for years striven hard to place before the public of Runcorn the disadvantages under which the ratepayers laboured in not possessing a good supply of books, on the ground that, "ignorance is the curse of God, Knowledge the wing wherewith we fly to Heaven," I will now be filled with hope that as matters have proceeded thus far, there is ground for anticipating a successful issue to the negotiations. It may be as well to state that the library possessed by the Institute might to be carefully examined before the purchase is completed, as some of the sets of books are defective. I know of instances where many an ardent reader has commenced to peruse some thrilling work, and when he has got through the first volume, he has found to his utter confusion that the library had lost the other volume or volumes, completing the series. One would have imagined that such defects as these in what is otherwise a very fair library, would have been remedied long ago, but the Runcornians are a race of men who do net often do any- thing in a hurry.

ROCK SAVAGE MISSION SUNDAY SCHOOL.—On Sunday two sermons were preached on behalf of this school by Mr. S. Walker, of Frodsham. The collection realised £3 3s. Mr. Jones acted as conductor of the singing. WIDNES AND THE BELLE VITE BRASS BAND CONTEST. —About 200 excursionists left Widnes for Belle Vue, Man- chester, via the London and North Western line, on Monday, to attend the now famous annual brass band con- test.

WIDNES AND THE ROYAL Vrsrr.—A large number of passengers left Widnes for Liverpool on Thursday, including about 140 by a special train run by the London and North- Western Railway. A CCIDENT AT MESSES. MATHESON'S WORE% WIDNES.-- On Monday, a lad named Wm. Brooks, of 48, Shaw-street, Runcorn, fell a distance of 18 feet whilst at work at Messrs. Matheson's, Widnes, and sustained concussion of the brain. He was taken to the Hospital and attended by Drs. McClellan and Pattison.

FARNWORTA AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY. - The 17th annual show of horned cattle, horses, pigs, poultry, and dogs will be held on Friday and Saturday next. £6OO will be distributed in prizes, and judging from the lovely weather with which we are having at the time of writing, itls highly probable that the committee will be favou'red with blue *skies and sunshine—two most important con- sideratipns in such an exhibition. A full report of Friday's proceedings will appear in the next issue of the Examiner.

STAR OF TEMPERANCE BRASS BAND.—On Saturday this band will play the following programme of music on the cricket ground, Widnes :—Overture, "Confidence," J. Hem- merle; selection, "Pirates of Penzance," A. Sullivan ; valse, " Susette," E. Telford ; fantasia, "Notre Chere Alsace," H. Kling; quadrille, " Queenstown," Dan Godfrey; selection, " Enura," Exudie ; march, "Distant greeting," A. Doring; polka, "Bijou," Harris; quadrille, "On the 1 banks of the Thames," H. Smith; schottische, "The rain- bow," H. Kleber ; National Anthem. Laricenram ANNUAL COUNTY Susurozr.—At the annual general session of county magistrates, held on Thurs- day, at Preston, the Earl of Derby was elected chairman of the court for the ensuing year, and Mr. J. T. Ilibbert, M.P., vice-chairman. Dr. Boyle subrnitted,a proposal for enlarg- ing the basis of the General Finance Committee of the county, with a view to give the committee a mere thoroughly representative character, but the motion fell to the ground for want of a seconder. The meeting resolved to increase the force of constabulary in most of the divisions of the county, the total increase being•two inspectors,l4 sergeants, and 102 constables.

MR. GLADSTONE AND LORD BRATICHAMP.—At the recent gathering of Birmingham Conservatives at Lord Windsor's seat, Rewell Grange, Lord Beauchamp asserted that Mr. Gladstone had put a penny on the income tax in order" to negotiate a treaty with France. A Bromsgrove Liberal having written to Mr. Gladstone calling attention to the statement, has received the following reply:—" 10, Downing. Street, Whitehall, September 3, 1881.—Sir, I am directed by Mr. Gladstone to acknowledge the receipt of your letter with which you favoured him on the 23rd ult., and to say that the statement which you aacribe to Lord Beauchamp with regard to the imposition of a penny on the income tax last year is a gross error. The penny was imposed to meet the charge necessary to abolish the malt duty and substitute a beer tax. I am, etc. HOP.acit SEYMOUR. RIOTING AT PRESTO:Y.—A serious riot broke out OD Tuesday night among some cotton operatives, employed by Messrs. Hawkins and Sons, at their mill in Adelphi-street, Preston. A reduction of 10 per tent., kis stated, was pro- posed on Tuesday morning to the warpers and winders, who refused at once to accept it. sod, after considerable disturb- ance, left the mill. The discontented hands, joined by hundreds of others, including a large proportion of weavers, assembled in the vicinity of the mill last night, and com— menced breaking windows, hundreds of panes being smashed. The office has scarcely a whole pane left. All the available police were hurried to the spot as soon as the disturbance was made known at the Police Station, and the riot was quelled about nine o'clock. The chief- constable narrowly escaped severe injury, a Dirge stone having whizzed close past his head. Several policemen have been more or less injured.

FATAL AaCTDENT TO A PAINTER AT SUTTON, ST. HELENS.—On Wednesday, an inquest was held at Sutton, before Mr. Driffield, coroner, on the body of John Leigh, nineteen years of age, a painter, residing in Church-street, Sutton.—From the evidence of Ellen Leigh, the wife of Robert Leigh, and mother of the deceased, and of Hugh Nash, Taylor's-row, Sutton, it appeared that on Friday deceased was engaged painting along iyith Nash and others at Mr. Blenkhorn's vinery., Deceased was standing on a footboard fixed above a cucumber frame, and in the course of the operations, Nash, who was engaged some yards away, heard a crash, and running to the place found deceased on his feet, but leaning against an adjoining building. Deceased appeared to be stunned and had a wound on his forehead, and he rubbed his head with his hand. He was taken home in Mr. Blenkhorn's trap, and Dr. Griffith's was sent for. Deceased did not recover, and died on Saturday evening. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

FURTHER SPREAD 07 PLEURO-PNEVACONLA AND FOOT AND Mows DrsEasz.—The Clerk of the Peace was on Saturday inftrmed that pleuro-pneumonia had extended to the farm of Mr. E. Lonsdale, Sharpies, and two cows had, been slaughtered. Foot and month disease has spread to the farm of Mr. Ward, Clayton-le Dale, one out of 24 being affected. On the farm of Mr. W. Yates, Aighton, Bailey, and Chaiglev, one out of nine has been affected; on the farm of Mr. E. Dolphin one out of IS, and on the farm of Mr. J. Leeming, same township, od4 out of 33. On Mon- ! day and Tuesday is was reported that three animals out of a heard of 35, belonging to Mr. Wm. Brown, Stanley House farm, Mellor, had been sia• ghtered, they being affected with pleuro-pneutnonia. Foot-and-mouth disease has manifested itself amongst the cattle of Ann Eastweod, Ridden farm, Aighton, Bailey. and Chaighley, were twq out of 25 are affected Mr. Thos. Holden, Whittam House, Whalley, one out of 19, and Mr. Thos. Wilkinson, Herd House Farm, Briercliffe, four out of:20. During last week 15 farms were affected with foot-and-mouth disease, thus bringing; the total member to 95. There have been 100 animals attacked, and 122 have recovered.
MR. A. U. YOUNG, MB., F.R.C.S. has been appointed lecturer on "Surgical pathology" at the Owen's College, Manchester.

Wanrwurrox CEurrEntr.—Returns of interments in the Warrington Cemetery during the week ending yesterday:— Adults, 7; children, 5; total 12. Mau Poottz's SMRVICES AT ST. HELENS. During the last three weeks special services have been held in the United Methodist Free Church, conducted by Miss Pooke, the Cornish Evangelist. These services, which have been productive of much good, were brought to a close on Tues- day evening, when, a farewell tea meeting was held in the above chapel. A large number sat down t 9 tea, and the meeting, at which speeches were delivered by Miss Pooke and several gentlemen, was very well attended, the chapel being quite full. • A ST. HELENS COUPLE'S GOLDEN WEDDING.—On Wed- nesday, the 50th anniversary of the marriage of Thomas and Margaret Dennett, 18, Brook-street, St. Helens. was cele- brated at their residence. A nnmber of the old couple's friends had tea together, and warm congratulations and good wishes for Mr. and Mrs. Dennert's Suture were tend..red to them. Both Mr. and Mrs. Dennett were born in enurch- street, St. Helens. and have lired in the town 311-jr life time, having lived twenty seven years at their prebent re- sidence in Brook-street. They were married at St. Michael's church In Liverpool, and their family consists of five sons and two daughters. ST. HELENS LIBEBAL CLUB AND THE IRISH LAND BILL.—Mr. H. R. Lacey, the chairman of the meeting of Liberals, held at the Liberal Club, during the late crisis on the Irish Land Bill, has received the following letter in re- pponse to the resolution of confidence in the Government, which was passed by the meeting and forwarded to Mr. Gladstone:—" 10, Downing-street, Whitehall, 31st August, 1881.—Sir,—I am directed by Mr. Gladstone to inform you that be has received the communication from the Liberal Club, St. Helens, on the subject of the Irish Land Bill, which you have done him the honour to forward to him.— I am, sir, your obedient servant, Honacz SEYMOUR."

Wednesday ... -01 Total rainfall at Friar's Green, to Sept. 7, 1881-2264 Sept. 7, 1880-1743 Height of gauge above sea level, 33 feet. MISSIONARY MEETING AT ST. HELENS.-011 Wed- nesday evening the Rev. George Peake, missionary, from Madagascar, delivered an address on missionary work in the Assembly-room, Brook-street, St. Helens. The Rev. R. J. Ward occupied tbe chair, and the room was about half full. Mr. Peake spoke of the habits and customs of the people of Madagascar, and alluded to the difficulties he experienced in acquiring a facility of speaking in that language. He gave an encouraging account of the pro- gress of civilisation amongst the people, which he said had been brought about by the establishment of Christian Mis- sions. At the close of the address Mr. Peake offered for sale a number of articles which he had brought from Madagascar. He stated that he had been at Newton-le- Willows recently, and there he sold £3O worth of articles so that the people Of Newton had had the " pick " of the col- lection.

• PRESCOT Runaz SANITANT Aurtrourrr.—A meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse on Thursday. There, were present Mr. J. T. Hall (in the chair), Messrs. J. Ranson, W. Swift, Eatock, Leatherbarrow, and Syder.— The Clerk read the minutes of a meeting of the Whiston Parochial Committee held on the previous Monday as follows t—Recommended that notice to abate nuisances be served upon Mr. Halsall, agent for cottage property in War- rington-road, and that if the nuisances be not abated within 24 hours the work to-be executed by the Authority, and the 'expense charged to the defaulter.—Recommended that the Surveyor confer with Mr. Barrow as to the best means of draining property near the chapel, and report at a future meeting.—Recommended that the owners of property opposite the Cerra Hotel be served with notices to connect the drains with the sewers of the Authority.—Mr. Leathet- barrow gave notice that at tha next meeting he would move that the present accumulation of ashes in Whistou should be removed by the Authority. This latter formation was believed to underlie the T, Jae, but to be overlapped, ISO as not to appear at the sur- f, cc, excepting at St. Helens Junction, where a marl bed and a colt sandstone beneath it, thirty awl izizzety feet thick ro- s,.ectively, and supposed by Messzs. Bin oey and Hull to be -rtnian marl and Lower Permian sandstone, were found in a quarry and a well. The so-called Permian beds, though ,nnconformable to the coal-measures, are quite conformable to the Trias, and are overlapped in consequence of an at- tenuation in themselves, and not 'through having suffered denudation before the Trias was deposited upon them. Con- sidering- also their lithnlogical similarity to the Trios, it seemsothat they should be classed with this formation,, rather than with the Permian. The Permian rocks are pro- bably absent west of Warringtontfor two boreholes at Park- side and Winwick, commencing in the pebble beds, entered the coal measures at 291 and 341 feet respectively without encountering them. The Tries contained a bed of shale about 30 feet thick, and was based by soft sandstone with twig-shaped concretions of iron pyrites. Like the spherical nodules of Collins Green, these probably owed their origin to the iction of coal-measure water, with sulphides in solution, acting on the colouring matter (peroxide of iron) of the Trim. The coal-measures consisted of purple and green marls, and at Winwick were associated with limestone. They, and the same beds found in the Farnworth boring, are precisely similar to the well-known Whiston limestone, and like it contain the nacroconchus carbonarius. These limestones are probably the equivalent of the Ardwick limestone series in the upper coal measures of Manchester, and may be found to be underlain by representatives of the coal seams which are found in connection with it. With- out doubt, they must be everywhere underlain by the whole of the productive middle coal-meanies. but at a great and unknown depth, though there is reason to believe that the thickness of barren measures would be less in Lancashire.

CONCERT AT PARR MOUNT, ST. HELENS.—A miscellan- eous concert was held on Monday evening, in Holy Trinity schools, in aid of the school fund. The concert was a very successful one; it may, indeed, be said to be the best that has been given in these schools for some years. The room which is unsuitable as a concert room, was well tilled, amongst those present being His Worship the Mayor (Aid. Harrison), the Revs. Canon Carr and W. Flaherty. The programme was divided into two parts, the first of which was composed. solely of sacred music, and the latter of secular compositions. The artistes were Mrs. Moss, soprano, of Mr. Charles Halle's Choir. Manchester: Miss Kay, soprano, of Wigan: Miss Smith, contralto, of St. Helens ; Mr. W. Greer, tenor, and Mr. Margeson, basso, of Wigan. Mr. James Dawber, of the Trinity College Local Choir, Wigan; and Mr. A. Kay, St. Helens, accompanied the artistes on the piano. Two anthems and the same number of glees were sung by the choir in a creditable manner, the first two being "Sing forth the honour of His name" and "Blessed be the Lord God." In the glee "Swiftly from the mountain's brow" a slight discord was noticeable at the finish. "The Foresters" was sung with spirit, and was well received by the audience. Mr. W. Greer, ably rendered the solo," Sound an alarm," from Handel's Judas Macca- beus, and in the second part " Madeline " was fairly ren- dered by him. Mrs. Moss and Miss Kay sang "0 lovely peace" in fine style, followed by Miss Smith, who is I possessed of a strong contralto voice, and who sang "Angels I over bright and fair" very nicely and carefully. This lady j also sang "The poacher's widow." Miss Kav:rendered the I solo from the Creation, "With verdure clad," in a very pleasing manner, and the way in which she sang" The King and the Beggar Maid" drew forth the applause of the audi- ence, who demanded an encore. Miss Kay responded to the call by singing "The Better Land." Mr. Margeson's pieces allotted to him were "Nazareth" and "The Bo'sen's Mate," the latter of which pleased the audience so much that he was obliged again to appear on the platform. He then sang "Pull way, my boys, pull away." Mrs. Moss sang with much feeling "I will extol thee," and, in response to an encore, bowed her acknowledgements. "Shadow Land," Pinsuti's sweet song, was also rendered by Mrs. Moss in beautiful style. A trio, "Queen of the night," was given by Mrs. Moss, Miss Smith, and Mr. Margeson. Mr. Dawber manipulated a piano solo in a manner which left no doubt as to his superior ability as a pianist, and he was loudly en- cored, but did not comply with the wishes of the audience. Mr. Fidler was announced to sing "The three little pigs " but that gentleman did not put in an appearance. James Kay conducted the choir.—The Rev. W. Flaherty thought they would not be doing their duty if they left with.- out giving an expression of the pleasure they had derived from the artistes, if such expressions were needed. He was pleased to see the Mayor of St. Helens present, for they. all , knew that he was a gentleman who would not withhold his patronage from any religious or good movement. He was sure they were all pleased to see the Mayor and his family with them, and also their old friend Dr. Carr. (Cheers.)— The Mayor briefly acknowledged the compliment.—Dr. Carr said he looked upon the people of Parr Mount as a branch of a big family, and that branch had grown bigger every year. Ile looked with great satisfaction upon what had been done at Parr Mount. There was no church there when he came to St. Helens, and now they had a church well filled. He never felt more at home than when he catne to Parr Mount, for his heart then got free, and his tongue was let loose. (Applause.)—The concert was brought to a close by the singing of the National Anthem,

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

INDEPENDENT METHODIST SCHOOL, GOLBORNE. On Thursday evening, a public meeting in connection with the I. 0. G. T. Ebenezer Lodge, Golborne, was held in the above school. There was a fair attendance, and all were much interested in the addresses delivered by Messrs. R. Yates, R. Johnson, and other gentlemen. Mr. Turton. of f3rolborne, officiated. GOLO3ORNE WESLEYAN CHAPEL. The Rev. J. M. Wahnsley, late of Leeds, and the newly appointed superin- tendent minister of the circuit, preached in the above chapel on Thursday evening, to a good congregation. He delivered an eloquent sermon from the 15th verse of the 3rd chapter of Proverbs. CHAPEL ANNIVERSARY SERMONS, GOLBORNE.—On Sun- day last two sermons were preached—afternoon and evening —in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Golborne, by the Rev. T. Swallow, of Liverpool. The discourses were listened to with ra,pt Attention by good congregations. The collections during the day amounted to the sum of £7 us. 4d. PRIMITIVE METHODIST SCHOOL, LOWTON.—On Wednes- day evening, a Band of Hope meeting was held in the above school, when Messrs. Yates and Williamson, of Golborne, gave stirring addresses. There was a fair gathering of mem- bers present, and both addresses were received with great applause. At the close, a hearty invitation was given to both gentlemen to favour them with another visit shortly, and both kindly accepted the same. GOLHORNE ASSOCIATION FOOTFALL CLUB.—A meeting in connection with the above oink was held in the Golborne Mechanics' Institution, on Friday evening, for the purpose of electing officers for the ensuing year, and for the enroll- ing of new members. A president and vice-presidents were elected, and also a committee of six persons formed. Mr. T. Berwick was unanimously elected captain. Mr. William Lay- bourne vice-captain, Mr. F. J. R. Williamson secretary, and Mr. Samuel Morris treasurer. About 30 new members were enrolled. A series of matches have been arranged for the season, of which due notice will be given. ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH, GOLHDRNE.—The annual charity sermons in aid of this mission were preached on Sun- day last. The preacher was the very Rev. Father Peter Paul, rector of the Passionist Community at Sutton, near St. Helens. The morning sermon was an eloquent discourse on the Companion of Christ, as shonin by many instances in His life; and the afternoon sermon was on "The Love of Christ," a-s shown by similar instances. The church was not very crowded either at the morning or the afternoon services, bnt those who were there gave very generously. The special objects of the collection were to remove a debt of £136 still on the mission, and then to build an infant school, the infants at present being in the same school room as the boys and girls of higher Classes. The choir was the usual choir of the church, and they sang remarkably well. The altar was very richly decorated with plants and flowers, sent for the occasion by the members of the con- gregation. GOLBORNE LIBERAL Assocramox.—The LOOM Of this association were opened on Wednesday last, when many members visited the place. At night the rooms were well Oiled, and all expressed their satisfaction at the comfortable appearance and cheerfulness of the place. Refreshments were provided, and many availed themselves of this pleasing feature of the Association. No intoxicating liquors are per- mitted to be sold on the premises. About 60 members were enrolled, and it is believed that in the course of another month upwards of 300 members will have joined the Asso- ciation. The earnestness of the Liberals of Golborne and district deserve ,the greatest praise, and there is not the slightest doubt that what they have set themselves to accom- plish they will succeed in doing. A billiard table and all the necessary requisites will be supplied shortly for the use of the members. A grand soirée will also be held shortly in connection with the Association, and other entertainments will be provided during the winter months. Liberalism is growing fast in the township and neighbourhood, and the borough franchise for the counties and redistribution of seats will be prominent subjects for discussion in the rooms of the Association. The benefits which Liberalism has con- ferred upon this country, in comparison to Toryism, will be freely discussed by the members, und all the young men of Golborne and district who are desirous of gaining a know- ledge of the political affairs of this country, and of improv- ing themselves morally, socially, and intellectually, will join the Association as early as possible. - - - •

div.head: WIDNLS MAIN SEWERAGE SCHEME.
div.p: WIDNLS MAIN SEWERAGE SCHEME.

This scheme is at the present time occupying so mach general attentioe on the part of the already heavily burdened ratepayers of the town of Widnes, that we feel justified in alluding to it at some length, although the sub- ject is not one of the most tempting in its character. Doubt- less the urgent needs of a main sewer is one of the principal causes of the notice which the question of sewerage attracts in Widnes at the present time. In considering the majority of cases in the past, we see very clearly that the builders have had to find outfalls for their drains in the nearest ditch.; whilst in others badly constructed temporary sewers have been provided by the Local Board, having their outfall in holes, been ci ael ditches.iniaeon::t,eiocse almost entirely b cr." Frequently qfenourgrectgaa;teetledtyse forgotten. ch.heeessisrei existence result snbuceleert nhsheetaerssmeeabsetedeat onndwt thihavehtahet ditches thus transformed into open sewers, emit stenches of a semi-pmsonous nature in certain instances. In others the tof properbi tr by w n yisne turning te hrs has e e rprecluding athemrproduced into fr miniature cat iotun nrs etcresunuevtbeitnnegir subterranean water thewcl want residents,e t Lakes in case of any heavy rain. The Local Board having observed that the lower part of the township was being trans- ferred into a large cesspool, first, apparently, began to think about the imperative necessity of a main sewerage scheme in 1872, and in the following year they decided to have a survey of the town made for drainage purposes. In 1874 the survey was began, but fearing that they would not be able to deal with the difficulties by which they were beset in time, they agreed upon a sort of relief sewerage scheme. This, however, only provided for the district of West Bank. The contract was let to Mr. Hunkin, of Liverpool, who com- pleted tan ye settled lower someportion pleted the work, and then brought a claim for extras, which number of floods caused by heavy rain; and in the following yortrhs e taof wtenr ewhair dp swboye asrubbi reacttieodn . t Ina year the Local Board again revived the proposal to construct a main sewer. Fortunately for the Board, Major Cross, the respected chairman, who is by profession an engineer, volunteered to give the proposal his careful consideration, and present his views in the shape of a report. After a few months had elapsed, some of the members manifested a little impatience at the report not having been submitted. Cer- tainly this would at first sight appearinexplicable on their part, when the fact is taken into consideration that the Board had for a period of six years shelved the consideration of the matter. Probably this state of feeling arose from a desire on the part of some of the representatives to show the ratepayers how zealous they were in a matter which so vitally affected the interests of the town! Ultimately, in the year 1878, the Board entered into an agreement with the representatives of the Leigh estate for the purchase of cer- tain land with the object of widening Victoria-road, and the former undertook to complete the construction of the main sewer as far as Sixim's Cross before July, 1883, or in default to pay the representatives of the estate between £2,000 and £3,000, that being the difference due to the estate. It was agreed that this payment should be remitted if the Board complied with the conditions of the agreement affecting the main sewerage works. It was indeed fortunate for the resi- dents of the township that an agreementof this description was entered into, as the Board could, under such circum- stances, no longer remain apathetic in regard to works upon which the public health depvded. In January, 1879, the Chairman of the Board submitted a report, which is the foundation upon which the scheme now under consideration by the public has been erected. It was as follows : " Drainage of Widnes.—To the members of the Widnes Local Beard.—Gentlemen,—l now fulfil my promise of bringing before you my views as to the main lines of drainage for this township. First, as to the position east of the St. Helens Railway. Ido not think there is any imme- diate necessity for extensive works in this district, and that a tew stoneware pipe drains into Bower's brook, and down Gorsey-lane to tb,e culvert under the canal, will, for the present, meet all demands. It will, however, sooner or later, be necessary to construct sewers; and I suggest that the western part of this district should be drained into Bower's brook, and the eastern down Gorsey-lane to the river. This will involve the construction of two main sewers. (A.) Commencing near the entrance to Hutchin- son's No. 2 works, and running along the canal bank and side of railway to Ann-street crossing, along Ann-street to Bower's brook; then as nearly straight as possible to the road above Vineyard crossing; along that road to near Appleton station; thence to Bower's brook at Plumpton's bridge, and finally along the brook course straightening it to the boundary of the township. This Beier would serve part of the district west of St. Helens Railway and to the east of Farnworth. There are no dilliculths in connection with it. (B.) A sewer from the rider, the whole length of Gorsey- lane, to the boundary of the township. This would be nearly a straight line, wita favourable giadients, and the cheapest sewer in the district. 2iel. As to the district south of Warrington and Grarston Railway. The sewering of a great part of this district is complete, and what remains to be dune calla tor no particular 'mention except that I believe part of the sewer along West Bank is defective and wants re-building; pipe drains or small sewers could then be put into it so as effectually ito drain this sec- tion. 3rd. There remains then the district west of St. Helens Railway. The first thing to fix on is the outlet for the main sewer. There are three points to choose from— (A) the present outfall for West Bank sewage, (B) Stew- arra brook, (C) the Marsh brook. (A). The outfall at West Bank is not now too large for the drainage of the southern section of the township. The sewer from Hutchinson-street to this outfall is very defective, and if this were selected for the main outfall, a new service would have to be constructed from the outfall to Victoria-road, and svould have to pass under the London and North-WesbAu Railway at Waterloo- road crossing, and the gradients from this last point to the river are so bad that no engineer would use them except on the direst necessity. (B). Steward's brook. There are fewer objections to using this as the main outfall, if from where it passes under the Ditton branch of the West Widnes Rail- way, it was carried straight to the river; but as the culverts under the London and North-Western Railway are defective, and, even if good, not of sufficient capacity, new sewers would have to be constructed from a point north of the old Warrington and Garston railway to the south of Acton and Ditton branch, and, with the marshy bottom, wouid make the construction both dangerous and costly. (C). There are no difficulties in construction with Marsh brook, and the ' gradients are favourable. I, therefore, advocate it as the main outfall, and suggest sewers. From the river to new Ditton-road 6by 4, length 1,020 yards, cost, say £3O per yard, £30,600. Ditton-road to Victoria-road 6by 4, length 500 yards, cost, say £l5 per yard, £8,850. Victoria-road to Kent's Crossing, 4ft. Bin. by 3, length 450 yards, cost, say £lO per yard, £4,500, Simms Cross to Plimpton's Cross- ing, 4by 2ft. Sin., length 1,210 yards, cost, say £8 per yard £9,880. To be done in 1879. Total cost, say £58,430. I would, however, at the same time, lay out a line of sewers thoroughly draining Newtown ; a main sewer from the Police Office along New-road to Appleton • another main sewer from bottom of Peel House-lane to Fern- worth Church; and a third from Ditton New- road along Lower House-lane. These, with the cross sewer, would, I think, thoroughly drain this section of the township, it being of course understood that they could be prolonged northwardc as far as necessary.—l sin, gentlemen, your obedient servant, JAMES Cnoss.-2nd January, 1879.— This report was lithographed, and circulated amongst the tmoemonbernsltOefrotthioenßooaorgdg.estletdsvbays afitre. r Kw ea ir,clt,s and adopted a gr, eeds utboj ebcyt Major Cross. The alteration was to the affect, that the route from Ditton-road, to the police station, should be changed, and instead of the sewer going the whole length of Ditton-road, as laid down in the report, it should branch off from Ditton-road, along New-road to Moor-lane, and thence along Moor-lane, to the police station.—Major CROSS in agreeing to this alteration, explained that his reason for choosing Ditton-road as the route, was solely attributable to the amount of chemical waste, which would have to be 'dealt with on the New-road. At a subsequent meeting, Mr. ' Copland, the sewerage engineer, was instructed to prepare the plans, and specifications, which would be required for th,e Local Government Board enquiry, and for the con- struction of the works. This took place on the 15th July, last year, on, the Board applying to. borrow £40,000. The scheme was then examinedin detail. Shortly afterwards the Local Board received power to borrow £38,000, for main sewerage purposes, that being the amount of the estimate prepared for borrowing powers. Owing to the state of trade, the Board, however, considered it advisable to postpone the commencement of the work at that time. In May last, the subject was again revived, and the necessity of advertising for tenders, once more refurred to. Probably this revival of the subject was due to the penalty which- the body would incur in the case of the Leigh estate, if they did not proceed with the work. At this meeting the chairman (Major Cross) said he had heard that Mr. Hieginson had a scheme for the main sewerage of Widnes, which that gentleman con- tendedm encou belonging approvedl b t° . I ofcarried by thoeußtoaard. ta lienseetrcnoestttotnheawnertehegiooenne already at the June meeting for Mr. Higinson to submit his scheme, and it was referred to a joint committee composed of Committeegentle- men for examination s botht is the hardly ersohnme.aoyanrd it y to part of the subject, as the course adepted by the Board must be fresh in the minds of our readers. Suffice it to say Health hell upon that the surveyor's scheme was rejected, and that of the Major's unanimously approved of by the Board. Let us hope that the time is not far distant when we shall see it carried out, to the lasting benefit of the town.

div.head: FRODSHAN.
div.p: FRODSHAN.

FRODSHANt AND HELSBY DRAINAGE BOARD.—A general meeting of the ratepayers of the Frodsham and Helsby drainage district was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Thursday evening, for the purpose of electing new members , Of tne Board, when there were present, Messrs. Jas. 11,7nolds ' (returning officer), Thomas Hignett, Henry Linaker, James Andrews, Thomas Arrowsmith, Thomas Lewis, F. Thornley, Thomas Davies W. E. Davies, H. Beswick, John Challoner, Ralph Bate, and Charles B. Linaker (clerk to the Board). The notice convening the meeting baling been read, the Clark read a letter from Mr. Henry Linaker declining to again serve as a member. The following gentlemen were ' proposed by Mr. Henry Linaker, seconded by Mr. Thomas Lewis, as members for the current year, viz., the Marquis of Cholmondeley, Messrs. Hayes, A. C. Talbot, E. A. Wright, James Reynolds, Thomas Hignett, John Higson, Ralph Bate A. White, F. Thornley, James Andrews, Vi illiam Booth, John Challoner, W. E. Davies, and James Percival. Mr. Arrowsmith, of Helsby, proposed Mr. Joseph Ellams as a member, hut not being seconded, the original motion was declared carried. A vote of thanks was unanimously accorded to the returning officer, on the motion of Mr. Henry Linaker, seconded by Mr. Thomas llignett.

div.p: LATEST NEWS.
In view of an immense religious jubilee in Limerick on Sunday next, all police and military will be confined to the barracks during the day.

The Central News is authorised to state Mr. Givan, has declined appointment as Assistant Commissioner under the Land Act. There will, therefore, be no vacancy for County Monaghan. A New Fork Herald telegram says a disturbance is crossing north of latitude 45, and will arrive on the North British and Norwegian coast between the 11th and 13th. Rains, south veering north-west strong winds or gales. Several villages have been destroyed by the forest fires in North Michigan, and more than 20 persons have been burned to death. Rain fell at Ottawa on Wednesday, and the bush fires in that immediate neighbourhood were ex- tinguished. In the middle States of NeW York there was intense heat on Wednesday, the thermometer reaching the highest recorded this season.

Messrs. Donald Carrie and Co., have undertaken to bring home from Natal a large number of the troopelately engaged in the Transvaal. The Royal mail steamer Balmoral Castle will leave Natal about the end of October, with 700 men. The Dublin Cystle will bring 700 at the end Gf November, and 300 more will be conveyed in another of the company's steamers.

Mr. Duckham, M.P., tenant fanner representative, speak- ing at an agricultural meeting at Craven Arms;yesterday, referring to the present Fair Trade agitation, said he must confess he was one of those who thought the present system was not a fair one. It could not be fair for one country to be handicapped against another as at present. He did not, however, believe protection could ever again be enforced in regard to corn and meat.

THE Mummer CEmmintratt Corrxru..—At the after- noon session of the Council there yesterday was a crowded attendance. The first paper on "Women and their work in Methodism" was read by the Rev. F. W. Bourne, of the Bible Christian Churches of Great Britain. The writer thought women Ehould only preach in exceptional circum- stances. The Rev. C. N. Payne, D.D., of the Methodist Episcopal Church, and several other speakers, gave great I credit to the women for their share of the work undertaken. The next paper was upon "Scriptural Holiness," and after a long discussion the conference adjourned.

The Trades Union Conference on the subject of Fair Trade reassembled yesterday, at Westminster Palace Hotel. Mr. Richard Hunt, representing the sugar industries of Bristol, presided, and advocated a duty upon foreign corn' but not upon that coming from the colonies. Mr. Fox, of Bristol, moved that the members of the conference, irrespective of politics, should co-operate to induce the Governments of Great Britain and the colonies to enter into negotiations for the abolition of all tariffs in restraint of free trade. Mr. Morrison seconded, but Mr. Hyde, of London, proposed an addition to the amendment, declaring that it would be un- wise of the Government to enter into any new treaty with France that did not ensure eqnal and just terms to both sides. After some discussion, however, the resolution as originally framed was unanimously agreed to, it being decided that the amendment would be out of place at this time. Mr. McStay, of Eiverpool, moved the next resolu- tion, declaring that in all imperial and international treaties when colonial interests were involved, the views of the Colonists themselves should be ascertained, which was car- ried. It was also resolved to found an organisation to carry out the resolutions passed at the conference. PRESIDENT GARFIELD.

LONG BRANCH, SEPT. 8, MIDNIGHT.—An official bulletin issued at 8.30 p.m. stated that the President's pulse at half- past five was 100, and that he had taken a libesal amount of both solid and fluid food. Since the issue of the evening bulletins the pulse rose to 108. The patient ate rather too I much at night, and experienced some discomfort from this cause. At a late hour the President was resting quietly. , President Garfield goes on improving. Drs. Reyintru,' Barnes, and Woodward have withdrawn from attending .the President, he'having expressed an opinion that his case can be equally well managed by fewer surgeons than the number I hitherto in attendance. Mrs. Garfield desired that the President's wishes should be complied with. Business was suspended in New York on Thursday, and prayers were offered up in the churches for the President's complete re- covery.

div.head: BOAT CAPSIZED ON THE MERSEY.
div.p: BOAT CAPSIZED ON THE MERSEY.

About half-past four (AI lock yesterday afternoon, a num- ber of persons embarked in boats. at New Brighton for the purpose of proceeding to inspect Her Majesty's ship Agincourt, which was lying in the Mersey. By some means or other a small beat, containing nine ladies and two gentle- men, cfune in contact with the paddle of a steamer, and was immediately capsized, the occupants being thrown into the water. Several of the occupants, however, managed to cling to the paddle, and were eventually picked up. A strong current was running at the time and two ladies were being fast carried away, when some of the men of the Agincourt gallantly jumped overboard and succeeded in rescuing the fair ones.
DEVASTATING FIRES IN AMERICA. FIVE VILLAGES DESTROYED. 100 PERSONS PERISHED.

A Daily News New York telegram of Thursday 'says:— Thursday proved to be hotter than the previous day. The thermometers in the city reached 100 k deg., the highest point for ten years. There were forty cases of sunstroke. Intense heat is reported from various points. IVashington was highest of all. There the thermometer was 104 k deg. This morning a cool breeze is blowing, and the approach of a cold wave is reported from the north-west. There was a heavy snowstorm in the Black Hills, Dakota, on Monday and Tuesday. The theremometer in the north-west was down to fifty. Devastating fires are reported in Northern Michigan. There has been no rain there for six weeks. The whole cowntry is as dry as tinder. A few days ago the forest fires started, and whole counties have been swept by the flames. Great stretches of farming country have been desolated, farmhouses, crops, barns, and fences being con- sumed. Many cattle perished, and alarming reports come of considerable loss of human life. It is said that as many as 100 persons perished. The fury of the flames was ap- palling. The farmers left everything, and fled for life. The weak and ailing were left to perish. Five Tillages are said to be totally destroyed, and several others practically. The whole country is so dark and smoking that breathing is difficult, and lights are constantly burning. The people are terrified, believing the end of the world has come.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskall. THE ALLEGED MALICIOUS WOUND/NG WITH A CAN.—Acm Wright, a married woman, of Pleasant-street, Lugsdale. was charged with having unlawfully wounded Sarah Ann Sant, a neighbour, by striking her on the bead with a lading-can. —Complainant said she was a married woman, and whilst passing thelonse of the prisoner on the previous morning, about half-past ten, she set upon her, without any provoca- tion, and hit her upon the head with a lading can. Some time previously they had had some words. The blow I which the prisoner gave her was, so severe that she fell down. She afterwards got up and closed with Wright, and in the course of the struggle they went into her (Wright's) house. Here the table was overturned, and prisoner again struck her two or three times. She found herself bleeding severely, and it was only with the assistance of Mary Ann Connor that she could walk as far as her own home. She -went to Dr. Cooper, who dressed her wounds, and she after- wards went to the police station and gave information.— Mary Ann Connor offered evidence in corroboration of this statement.—Dr. O'Keeffe said complainant visited his sur- gery on the sth inst. He examined her and found an in- cised wound, 1 inch long, upon her forehead, and penetrat- ing to the bone. On the left temple there was another wound, about an inch in length, and it had divided a small artery from which blood flowed very profusely. When the woman catne to him it was quite evident she had lost a large quantity of blood, as her hair and clothes were matted. Such wounds might easily have been caused by an instru- ment like a can, and there was a spot of blood on the bottom of the can with which complainant alleged she bad been struck. From his own knowledge of her constitution, he was of opinion that the wounds were dangerous, as she was in the habit of taking alcoholic liquor. Considerable violence must have been used to cause them.—P.C. Clark- son said he apprehended the prisoner, who was in drink at the time. On the following morning he charged her with unlawfully wounding, and she replied that complainant came into her house and struck her first—ln answer to the formal charges, prisoner told the Bench similar story to that she had related to the policeman, and added that she did not 'know whether she stfuck complainant with the can or not in the struagle.—Mr. Gaskell said the wounds were evidently of a serious nature and he considered the case , one which should go for trial. He therefore committed the prisoner to take her trial at the quarter sessions. WEDNESDA.T.—Before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell, junr„, (chairman), and W. Brook.
