WARRINGTON TOIPN COUNCIL SPECIAL AIEETING. A special meetind of the Council was held on Tuesday, to sanction the payment of a contribution towards the main- tenance in a certified industrial school of four boys, named Thos. Brooks, John Killala, John Healey, and John Lingard. There were present the Mayor (presiding), Aldermen Webster Kean, Harrison; Councillors Brown, Woolfall, Caldwell, Litton, Monks, Ashton, Greening, Wallington, Greenall, Ridgway, Dixon, Whittle, and Platt; Messrs. J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (borough ' treasure!), and J. H. Gornall (medical officer). The requisite orders were made. The monthly meeting of the Council was afterwards held, when, besides those members above named, there were pre- sent Aldermen Davies, Burgess; Councillors Broadbent, Percival, Milner, Fairclough, Francomb, Jeans, and Mr. T. Longdin (borough surveyor). ILLNESS OF THE TOWN CLERK. The MAYOR said he was sorry he had received a telegram from the Town Clerk, stating that through illness he was unable to attend the meeting. THE COUNCIL AND PRIVATE UNDERTAKINGS. The MAYOR read a communication from the hon. secre- taries of the Workmen's Club Bazaar, respectfully request- ing the Mayor, Aldermen, and Councillors to follow the ex- ample of the Mayor and Corporation at the Workmen's Bazaar held 20 years ago, and be present at the opening of their bazaar. They proposed meeting Sir R. A. Cross, who had undertaken to open the bozaar, at the Mayor's Parlour (which his worship had promised the use of), and to walk with him to the Volunteer Drill Hall. As the Workmen's Bazaar had no connection with any political body it was earnestly hoped that the Council would accede to this, the unanimous request of the committee. The MAYOR said he should be glad to attend and assist Sir Richard in opening the bazaar. He went to a concert in , connection with the club the other evening, and there was a large attendance of respectable working men, who seemed to enjoy themselves very much. If thoroughly carried out there was no doubt the concerts would be of benefit to the town. He begged to move that the Mayor, Aldermen, and Councillors who could conveniently attend, do so at the Mayor's Parlour on the day named. An inaudible remark was made by Councillor Mon ks,

accommodation be required. Several recommendations of the Hospital Sub-Committee were approved and adopted, including one that the matron's salary be increased from £3O to £4O per annum, such increase to commence on September 29th, 1881. The minutes also contained cor- respondence between the Local Government Board and the committee on the subject of the alleged nuisance at Longford depBt, which appeared in our columns last week. Aid. BURGESS moved the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor Monks seconded the motion, and said he felt himself in a very unsatisfactory position, eoecially in re- gard to the removal of patients to the Infectious Diseases Hospital. He believed the action of the committee was certain to defeat the object they had in view, and that it was being taken in a manner that was not altogether warranted by the facts of the case. (Hear, hear.) They might carry out theories so far as to become ridiculous, and he thought it just possible they might become such enthusiasts in sani- tary science as to be enthusiasts merely, and not thoroughly Practical in their efforts. He was afraid, in regard to the Infectious Diseases Hospital, they were fast drifting into that positon. He did not wish to hamper the committee, but he should like an expression of opinion from the members of the Council, and if they endorsed the policy of the committee in trying to compel the removal of every case to the hospital, he would loyally do what he could to carry out the instruc- tions of the Council. If, on the other hand, there was suffi- cient expression of opinion to justify him irr continuing the opposition which he had felt it his duty to make, he should do so until the whole question came fully and fairly before the Council, as he thought it very likely would do at the next meeting. He believed the hospital was now full. They had had two special meetings to consider what steps should be taken to increase the accommodation. He agreed with the committee up to a certain point that isolation was desirable, but when the disease assumed a form in which it could be dealt with at borne, he thought it was better the cases should be left there, anti the patients left in charge of those persons whose eesponsibility and duty it was to attend to them. He was afraid it was a sort of semi- pauperism. They might say what they like about it, bu so long as any :one was fed clothed, nursed, and attended to at the expense of the, rates, it smacked very much of pauperism to his mind. Jlear, hear.) He hesitated very much as to whether the committee were exactly on the right lines in compelling the removal of cases to the hospital. He was inclined to think it was not a desirable thing to loosen those bonds which made families take care of the sick and attend to them; and he thought they would not need to exercise the compulsory powers soon, because they would have people bringing their children to the hospital without very much difficulty. He thought they would find by and by they could get that class to attend to, and the hospital would simply become a huge nursing establishment supported at the expense of the rate- payers. He did not find fault with the principle. In all these matters they must have a large discretionary power. But the question he raised was that in his opinion the whole thing wasbeing done with a zeal and with an enthu- siasm that was not at all desirable. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR: I think you are going off the minutes. It is all very well to keep the hospital to the fore, but you know we are going according to the Act of Parliament. We have nothing on the minutes. Councillor MONKS : I contend that we are not, Mr. Mayor. The MAYOR : I don't see how you can second the minutes by refusing to join the committee without you bring forward some amendment. Councillor Moems : Well, it beats on the whole question ; and I know that on the committee it is construed that may means must, but if I un- derstand the word may, it gives discretion. (Laughter.) I know very well it was stated at the Council meetipg, when the byelaws were made, that may meant may, and not must, and if it is now sought to construe the word may eo mean must, somebody is in fault, because we certainly understood may to mean may, which means that if it is per missive. I am ip your hands, Mr. Mayor, and sit down- because I can take the matter up at the next Council meeting. The MAYOR :Yes, I think it will be better if you make no comments upon it. Of course, all these cases are left to the discretion of the magistrates. by Act of Parliament? Councillor MONKS: That is so where there is a refusal on the part of parents to allow the removal, but not otherwise. Councillor KEAN said they were all agreed on one point, that the isolation of infectious cases, was very desirable. The question was, had the patients who had been removed to the hospital, got that isolation. He had heard of children who when in a couvale4ent state, after suffering from fever, yet remained with the sick children night and day. If that were true it showed a bad state of things. Alderman DAVIES rose to a point of order. The MAYOR : I was just going to stop Alderman Kean. Councillor SUTTON said what concerned the Council more particularly was the providing of additional accommodation in the shape of cots for the hospital. He did not see that they could go beyond that, and if Councillor Moaks desired to bring forward a motion to prevent the compulsory removal of patients to the hospital he, no doubt, could do so, and bring it before the Council on another occasion. He might rergark that they had already had one or two propositions On the subject, which had failed, simply because members (and perhaps Councillor Monks was one of them) left the room, and there was no quorum to discuss them. The minutes were passed. GAS COMMITTEE. The minutes stated that the average illuminating power of the gas for the fortnight ended 29th July was equal to 18.78 candles; for the fortnight ended 12th August 1913 candles; and for the fortnight ended 20th August 19.2 can- dies. It was resolved that the tender of Messrs. Fletcher, Burrows, and Company, for the supply of 7,000 tons of coal, accoiding to specification, be accepted; and that the Council be recommended to appoint Alderman Harrison a member of I the committee in the Place of Mr. Hind. On the motion of Alderman WERSTER, seconded by Councillor MILNER, the minutes were confirmed. TIIE TOWN CLOCKS. At a meeting ef the General Purposes Committee, on the 29th August, it was resolved that the tender of Mr. George Blackhurst, for the care of the town clocks according to the specification prepared by the Borough Surveyor, for the sum of £24, for twelve months from the let September next, be accepted, the Corporation having power to determine the agreement on giving one month's notice, in case the clocks are not kept in order to the satisfaction of the Corporation. Resolved, that the following estimate of the expenditure for the ensuing half-year be approved :—Borough rate account: Maintenance of buildings, £5O; municipal election expen- ses, £200; sundries, £150; £4OO. Improvement rate account: Half-year's care of Trinity and Market Gate clocks, £l2; gas to illuminate dials of Trinity Church clock, £2O; sundries, £lO. The minutes were adopted on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Councillor FeinerorGie. The Council then rose.

THE HEAVY TAXATION AT WIDNES. Sir,—May we ask if the ratepayers of Widnes are clearly aware how heavily they are taxed, We may safely presume that they grmerally are not, or that their patience and pay- ing capacity are most exemplary. Let them study this. We have now a Local Board rate of 25. 6d. per £ for eight months, equal to 3s. 9d. per £ for a year; and a general district rate of 2s. 4d. for eight months, equal to 35. 64. per £ for a year, or the sum of 7s. 3d. per £ per year, on ' rateable value, which is generally nearly equal to the amount of rent paid on. Plainly, thus we pay 36± per cent. on rateable value, or nearly 275. 31. per £of rentals. What have landlords been thinking of to allow their property to he thus depreciated, and how long will the patient taxpayer be able to stand this? It is to be hoped that, like Bob Lovre's bullocks, they will some day find their'power and show it by returning men to the Local Board, rtc., who will really practice economy after election and not preach it so much before. We are promised a grand drainage scheme—only a mere trifle of £20,000„ Of course the flourishing state of business in the district will enable an additional rate of 2s. Gd. per £to be cheerfully paid. Can information be Lad as to why the time covered by the rates is so carefully kept out of the demand notes? Is this not something like blinding the public? Let the ratepayers ponder these things before next election. Their interests and business are seriously menaced by the rash expenditure that has pre- vailed, ergo flagging round a grass field, &c., while the poor denizens of 'Newtown struggle over the corduroy pavement. —Faithfully yours, DROMIO.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY 'SESSIONS. VEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. G. Artingstall and Mr. Peter Stubs. FRUIT STEALING.—Five youths named Isaih Hobson, Edward Barker, Samuel Farnell, Albert Stokes, and Henry Parnell, were charged with stealing a quantity of pears from the garden of Mr, William Beamont, Orford Hall, doing damage to the amount of ss. Hobson, who had been twice previously charged with theft, was fined 10s. and costs, or, a month's imprisonment; Barber and Farnell were fined ss. and costs, or a fortnight's imirisonment ; and Stokes and Parnell were ordered to receive six strokes with the birch- rod. RAILWAY PROSECUTION. A well dressed young man named Joseph Lythgoe was charged with using abusive and obscene language on premises belonging to the Cheshire Lines Committee, at Glazebrook. Inspector Hanks said the defendant alighted from a Manchester train at Glazebrook, on the 30th ult., and in the altercation with the station master used some very foul language. Application had been made to the manager and the defendant had amply apolo- gised, and promised to pay all costs. With the permission cf the Bench, the case was withdrawn. BREACH OF THE HIGHWAY ACT BY A WARRINGTON TOWN Comscrurou.—Richard Francomb, coal agent, Warrington, and a town councillor, was charged with allowing his carts to be used on the highway without having his name painted upon them.—P.C. Macfarlane, on Monday, the 29th ult., saw one of the defendant's carts without his name painted upon it, on Padgate-road, Poulton, and on the following day he saw another in the same state. He spoke to the carter, who said that the clerk was painting the name on the cart when Mr. Francomb told him not to do so, as the printed card which was nailed upon it was quite sufficient. —Mr. Francomb said be had given an order to Mr. Whittle for two boards to be painted, and he thought the printed card would do for a few days. He did not think he was breaking the law.—The case was dismissed on pay- ment of costs.—Mr. Francomb : lam much obliged to yon, gentlemen, but it is terribly straining the law.—Mr. Arting- stall : Oh, no no; it is you who broke the law. A YOUNG no, Naylor, a girl 12 years of age was charged with stealing from the till of Michael Sculley. :grocer, Winwick-road, Orford.— Superintendent Jackson said that on Saturday, the 3rd inst., prisoner went into the prosecutor's shop to purchase some small articles, and tendered in payment a florin. Mrs. Sculley had not sufficient money to change that coin, and sent the girl to do so. When the girl returned Mrs. Sculley was not in the shop, but coming in shortly afterwards the girl handed her the change, and irnmediently went away. Looking into the till Mrs. Sculley immediately missed a half sovereign, and went to the house of the girl's parents to make inquiries. She denied any knowledge of the theft, and the money could not be found. Afterwards she admitted stealing the half sovereign and twopence, and pointed out the place where the money was concealed.—The Bench ordered the girl to be imprisoned one day as she had been locked up since Monday. A GLAZEBROOK Scm,mar.-IMoses Higgs, an employe cn the Cheshire Lines at Glazebrook, was charged, on remand, with unlawfully wounding Joseph Allen, a coal agent of that place, by striking him with an iron shovel at Glazebrook station on the 3rd inst.—Prosecutor did not op- pear, and Mr. Hanks, who represented the company, said he did not think he would, as the case was so very disgraceful. —Mr. Slater, who appeared fcr the prisoner, said the out- lines of the case were these. The prosecutor was a man of very bad character about Glazebrook, and had been mixed up with various scandals. A few months ago it was rumoured that the prisoner's wife had been seen with the prosecutor frequently, and that on more than one occasion he had entered the house when the prisoner was on duty. The scandal growing past bearing, the prisoner gave the prose- cutor a severe castigation. There was a gentleman from the company present to speak to the excellent character of the prisoner. As the prosecutor did not appear, he asked that the prisoner be discharged.—The Bench discharged the prisoner, and made an order on the prosecutor to pay the costs.

div.head: WARRINGTON LICENSING MEETING.
div.p: WARRINGTON LICENSING MEETING.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Licensing Com- mittee for the hearing of new applications, was held on Tuesday. There were present—Alderman Davies (chair- man), Alderman Holmes, and Councillors Milner and Fairclough.

OFF LICENSES. The following shopkeepers applied for licenses to sett beer to be consumed MI the premises :—Peter Knight, 7, Princes-street; William Hastings, Liverpool-road; Thomas Foster Nevins, Norman-street; Patrick Farrell, 59, Elles- mere-street ; Henry Corney, Orford-lane; and James Lea, Winwick-road.—Mr. Slater (Messrs. Robert Davies and Ce.) appeared for the first three named, and Mr. Moore for the others. The application of James Lea was granted, Hastings and Farrell were refused, and the others adjourned for the premises to be valued by the overseers' representative. A retail license to sell wine and spirits was granted to Charles Holland, liquor dealer, Froghall-lane, and a wine license to James Rathbone, of the Farmers' Arms, Dallam-lane. APPLICATIONS REFUSED. Mr. Slater appeared for Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. to ask for the removal of the license of the Pelican vaults, in Buttermarl-et-street, to an hotel to be erected in Hoyle-street. It was nine years since the application was first made, but the Bewsey-road of 1881 differed much from the road as in 1872, the population in the neighbourhood having increased by about 4,000 persons. There were no public-houses in Bewsey-road, and the Coopers' Arms in Bewsey-street was 1150 yards from the proposed erection. He mentioned the advantage it would be to free Buttermarket-street, which was overcrowded, Of a beerhouse, and confer it on a first-class hotel in Bewsey-road, the estimated cost of which was £4,500. Mr. Ridgway said Mr. Slater had helped him considerably in epposing not only his own, but one of which notice had been given for, The Grove. From their worships' local knowledge he was sure they would agree with him in say- ing that during the last twelve months the population of that neighbourhood had decreased, and was now much less that formerly. The number of empty houses was very great. He had a memorial signed by all the owners of pro- perty in Bervsey-road, with two exceptions, opposing both applications. In the district there were 24 out-doorlicenses, and ten in the immediate neighbourhood.—Mr. Slater under- stood the great majority of the outdoor licenses were under the control of Messrs. Greenall, and if this license was granted they would be willing to suspend the outdoor licenses, and shut the places up.—Mr. Ridgway said the Bench could hardly accept that statement as being worth anything, as the people holding the off licenses could apply to have the same houses licensed again.—On behalf of Elijah Lawton, Mr. Gee applied for a heerhouse license for The Grove, Bewsey-road, for which an off license was now held. This application, he said, could not be considered like the one just beard, as the house already existed. The aPplication had been made three or four successive years, and he hoped his client's perseverance would be rewarded with success. Applicant was the holder of a 2iX days' license to sell beer off the premises, and all he asked for was a six days' license to sell On the premises, consequently there would be no Sunday drinking, usually the great objection to these houses. Since the application was last made 400 buildings for workmen had been erected, and since the plan ef the borough engineer was made in 1875 there had been four streets built, so that within the last four or five years there had grown up in the imme4iate neighbourhood a large number of workmen's houses.—Mr. Ridgway said the house being 40 yards from the road and out of sight was one of his principal objections, and thought the Bench would agree that licensed houses should be in the road where they would be wider the strict surveillance of the police, and also pasrsers by. If the men at the iron works were taken ill, stiiits were kept on the works to aid their maladies. The license was opposed by owners of property in Bewsey-road, and he also had a memorial against it from a large number of working men at the ironworks of Messrs earson and Knowles.—Both applications were refused.

div.head: TRAV-ELS IN THE EAST.
div.p: TRAV-ELS IN THE EAST.

BY A SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. [SPECIAL.] No. XV. JERUSALEM (ColeriNunn). It was two lays after we arrived that we visited the Place of Wailing expecting to witnesssorne heartrending pictures of Jewish woe. I must say I felt a little be-fooled, anal a little ashamed to be one of quite a number of people who stood looking on. The wailing was not wild, but done eta whisper, by five or six beggarly-looking men and women, who stood with their faces to the holes in the wall muttering their prayers. My first thought:was, why these poor creatures must be paid for this. To keep up the pre- tence of Jewish woe for the loss of their city and temple, their richer brethren, who would be ashamed to come here themselves, send these poor people to carry on the farce. I was not then aware of the abject pauperism to which European charity had reduced the Jewish population, but in view of it I feel satisfied myimpression was correct, namely, that the wailing is done to order. The place is interesting as showing the utteridestruction which fell upon the temple and its surrounuing walls. The stones, inte wpose open joints the Jews direct their prayers, are built in a way which must remove from the mind of every beholder the idea that, in their position, they form the base of an original structure. The size and appearance of the stones indicate a grand origin, but their rude and disordered putting together makes it quite evident that they had at one time been thrown down and afterwards rebuilt. Accompanied by a cawass, a military attendant of the English consul, we visited the Hamm or temple area—a privilege denied to any but Maho- rnedaies previous to the Crimean war, and now only accorded to those who can apply to the itching palm of Turkish officialism a " sovereign " ernolient. If obtrusive lying drives away almost every holy thought as you stand before the so-called Christian shrines, the universal substi- tution of the name of Mahomet for that of Christ on this, the site of His own Father's house, and the consequent pre- valence of the sensuous over the spiritual, are equally unfavourable to profitable Christian reflection. You stand within the place and tread the very' ground over which the feet of a David, a Solomon, a Hezekiah, a Jeremiah, a Nehemiah have daily trod—over which, indeed, the voice of the Son of God hath sounded in withering anathemas or accents of tenderest love, and yet a sort of paralyses settles upon the imagina- tion, and the chill upon the heart. You come to see! and what do you see? Why, mosques and Makometanisrn, Minerets and Muezzims, Moslems, and Mecca worship, all confounding and confusing the spiritual sense, and making it almost impossible for poor humanity to shake off the incubus, or seize with any power, the matchless associations, and sublime history of this renowned place. It was here the Lord made the place of His feet glorious. It was here the tribes of Israel gathered to " rejoice before the Lord," and to "lee His beauty in the sanctuary." Within this grand enclosure, and with "the mountains round about Jerusalem," looking down upon it, the mae.- nificient Temple of Solomon stood and drew the wonder and envy of the whole world. And now—the Mosque of Omar! the Dome of the Rock! very beautiful the Mosque—very wonderful the Rock! But I must leave the connoisseur to get into raptures over the one, and the unreasoning devotee to bow down before the other. A low octagonal structure covered with blue and white tiles, even though its black dome, shining beneath an eastern sun, is the largest and noblest in the world, does not impress me with its mag- nificence. And when its chief attraction inside is a rock with a circular hole in the top, which they say was pierced through by Mehemet from a cavern below as he flew up to heaven on horseback, and which rock would have followed him if it had not been held down by the angel Gabriel, whose finger-Prints are still clearly visible, 1 am satisfied to leave it for other hearts and other pens to grow hot and eloquent in its praise. But, stripping that wonderful of its Moslem associations, can it be possible that it is, after all, the very threshing-floor of Oran the Jebusite (2 Chron. Ili. 1); or the altar, which was on Moriah (Gen. xxii.). upon which Abraham offered up his son Isaac! The b are possibility of its being either one or the other gives a sacredness to the snot. At the south end of the temple area, and behind the Mosque of Omar, is the more ancient Mosque of El Aksa, into which we had scarcely entered when we had to be hurried by our guide across its spacious aisles into the recesses of a corridor to avoid being noticed by the conductors of a funeral pro- cession which followed us into the place with its wilcLand noisy rites. From behind the pillars we saw it was ushered in by three or four Arab boys who came leaping in at the door, springing with their bare feet over the thick Turkish carpet. 'No one seems to know to what excess of violence their hatred of Christian people may hurry the Mussulmans, especially if they imagine any intrusion upon their funeral obsequies. To the south-east of the El Aksa are the cele- brated substructions, to which we descend by a staircase of thirty or forty steps. In a chapel at the bottom we are shown the " Cradle of Christ," which they say was occupied by the babe after His presentation in the temple, when Simeon blessed Him. By these substructions the Harem is carried over the side of the hill so as to give it squareness and increase its area. They consist of about one hundred simi-circular vaults, resting on square piers, which are com- posed of drafted stones, never dressed for their present pur- pose, but which must have formed either much grander sub- structions in early times, or the walls of some splendid building. It is evident that in the days of the Crusaders the vaults were used by the Templars as stables, inasmuch, as holes and rings are found driven through the corners of the pillars to which the horses have been attached. Looking upwards, we see the immense roots of the trees penetrating through the stones, and twisting into the joints at the bend of the arches. These belong to the trees growing on the temple area above. We also visited the wonderful quarries, which run in, from near the Damascus gate, a long way under the city, entered by a low doorway through which you have difficulty in creeping. We saw the beauti- fully white stones standing on end half-quarried, and wondered whether they had been intended for Solomon's Temple, m bore a later date. At the risk of being thought prolix, I must say a word about the walls that surround the modern Jerusalem. Having done so I shall bring my account of the city to a close, feeling nevertheless that I could dwell much longer on its sweet and sacred memories. The archos3logist must find it very difficult to fix the periods at which the various stones found a resting place in the motley architecture. The materials are of the most compo- site character. Stones of immense size at the base are surmounted with mere rubble built in with bigger stones, and here and there with pieces of beautiful marble, granite, and porphyry columns, the whole evidently utilized from the ruins of the ancient city, and probably of the Temple. Some of the lower stones are very large and are dressed with bevelled or rebated edges. I measured one ; it was 235 t 91n. long, aft. 3in. deep, and was projecting from a part of the walls which was set back sft. ein. If such stones com- posed the Temple, well might the prediction of the Saviour that during that generation not one stone should be left upon another, appear like an idle threat, for it seemed an utter impossibility. Yet it is recorded that the Romans, after razing the Temple to the ground, actually drove a ploughshare across the ruins as if the prediction should not want the most literal fulfilment. Regarding the solidity of the walls Josephys says: "Titus gave orders that the batter- ing rams should be brought and set over against the western edifice of the inner temple; for before these were brought the firmest of all the other engines had battered the wall for six days together without ceasing, without making any im- pression upon it; but the east largeness and strong connec- tion of the stones was superior to the engine, and to the other battering rams also. Other Romans did indeed under- mine the foundations of the northern gate, and, after a world of pains, removed the outermost stones, yet WAS the gate still upheld by the inner stones, and stood unhurt till the workmen, despairing of all such attempts by engines and crows, brought their ladders to the cloisters." The Lord's Day we spent at Jerusalem must be ever dear to our hearts as having afforded 'as the opportunity of celebrating the Lord's death within a few paces of the spot on which His decease was accom- plished. My own impression is that we were so near to Calvary and Joseph of Arimathea's tomb that the ground on which we stood might have shaken with the dying agonies of the one, and been illuminated with the resurrec- tion glory of the other. In the early part we wondered over two or three low hills, at the foot of which our tents were spread; any one of these, we thought, would answer the commonly received idea of Calvary. We saw caves, too, on their rocky sides of tomb like appearance and dimensions, and while we thought of the possibility of one of these being the tomb of Joseph we scarcely dared to express it. With hearts subdued and impressed by contact with scenes to which in imagination we had so often turned, to which millions of the human family daily and hourly direct the eye of faith, and on which for once only in our mortal life we could hope to look; we sat down on this "pearl of days," to remember the Lord's death in grateful and loving obedience to his dying command. May our observance of it strike a key-note whose tones shall vibrate until pure Christianity shall again lift up its voice in that ancient land, and may the hymns we sang before we went out to the Mount of Olives, and as we stood upon it, awaken echoes whose music shall swell until hosannas louder and sweeter than of old, reverberate through the hills and valleys of poor forsaken Palotine! (To be continued next week.) •

div.head: FRODSTIAM.
div.p: FRODSTIAM.

SUNDAY SCHOOL SERMONS AT ROCK SAVAGE, CLIFTON.— The first anniversary sermons in connection with the Rock Savage Mission school were preached on Sunday by Mr. Samuel Walker, of Frodsham. The services were held in Mr. Stokes' house, and were very well attended. The mis- sion has done a good work since it commenced, as there are \ about 50 scholars on the books, and the children present joined very heartily in the hymns selected, which they ap- peared to know thoroughly. The collections amounted to ' nearly 13. PRIVET Hawn MOTH.--A. fine specimen of this moth has been found in a potato field at Frodsham, and is now in the possession of Mr. Charles E. Linaker. PROLIFIC POTATOFS.—The following satisiactory results have been obtained by a Frodsham gardener. A seedling potato 4 oz, was planted and yielded 65 which weighed 6lbs. 13 oz., and on these being set they yielded 114Ibs. A mag- num bonum potato 9oz. was found to produce 13lbs.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 10, 1881 RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 10, 1881 RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

_ IMPROVEMENT COIIMISSIONERS- The monthly meeting was held on Monday. Dr. Steele presided, and there were also prestat. Messrs. Norman, Tay- lor, J. 1. Speakman, Shaw, Lake,Trandley, Briscoe, Collier, Meadowcroft, McDougall, Linaker (law-clerk), Brookes (secretary), and Barker (surveyor). THE COST a THE ANNUAL ELECTION The CHAIRMAN reported the result of the election, and said that his costs, as Returning Officer, had been £lO lie. Bd.—The account was passed, on the proposition of Mr. NORMAN, secondea by Mr. J. J. SPEARMAN. RUNCORN AND THE CHESHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY. I The CHAIRMAN reported that he had received the follow- ing (copy) letter:—" Cheshire Agricultural Society, Estate Office, Oulton Park, Tarporley, 2nd September, 1881. Dear , Sir,—Ever since your defeat in November last there has been a steons, and growing feeling amongst the members of the Cheshire Agricultural Association that, if desired by the Runcorn people, our next year's show ought to be at Runcorn. lam quite sure there will be no difficulty at our next general annual meeting in securing a majority of votes in favour of the show for 1882 being held in your town if sufficient funds can be raised by a loc3l committee to guar- antee a big show for two days. lam not writing this letter in my official capacity as secretary, but as a private member of the society, having so repeatedly heard other members express their intention of voting with you should you send a deputation to our general meeting, which will be held in November next.—Yours truly, W. BECKETT."-Dr. Steele (continuing) said the members would remember that last year, when the Board applied that the show might be held in Runcorn, the vote went in favour of Sandbach, at which result they, no doubt, felt a little grieved. He was of opinion that it was very desirable the exhibition should be held in Runcorn next year, and, if they desired that con- summation, they must, of course, take the necessary steps as the annual meeting of the committee would be held in November.—After a few remarks of a conversational char- acter, it was unanimously decided, without the passing of any formal resolution, that a meeting of ratepayers should be called to consider the desirability of making application that the next show of the society should be held in the town.

MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. This report was presented by Dr. R. H. Mouritz, and showed that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 14, representing a death rate of 11 per 1,000 per annum. Of the above deaths five were due to pulmonary diseases, two to abdominal com- plaiqts, and two to cancer. Scarlatina, convulsions, etysipelas, phthisis, and diseases of the heart accounted for one each. Of the deaths three were those of infants below one year. One inquest had been held, making the total deaths 15.

HIGHWAY COMMITTEE. The minutes stated that a resolution bad been passed that the officials of the Board be required to lay before each com- mittee "copies of any correspondence relating to any business belonging thereto." A circular had been received from the deputy clerk of the peace, with reference to main roads, recommending that application be made for the following to be declared such: Halton-road, Bridge-street, High-street, Lowland's-road, and Holloway and Weston roads. The committee had had an interview with Mr. H. White, as to the erection of his office in contravention of the building bye-laws, and a resolution had been passed that in consideration of his coating the building with sheet iron and giving an undertaking to remove ta structure at a month's notice, if required, the summons against him be withdrawn. Instructions had been given to the law clerk to communicate with the estate agent of the L. and N.-W. Railway Company, with regard to the railway bridge slope. —Mr. Norman moved and Mr. Briscoe seconded the resolu- tion in favour of passing the minutes.—After some discus- sion, Mr. SHAW moved and Mr. MEADOWCROFT seconded an amendment in favour of the resolution concerning officials and the correspondence of each commitiee being struck out. —The amendment was lost and the original resolution car- ried by a considerable majority. THE CANAL BOATS' ACT. The Canal Boats and Hospital Committee reported that a letter had been received from the School Board, expressing approval of the educational clause in the Canal Boats' Amendment Bill. A resolution had been passed that the roof of Waterloo House be renaired. The deputation ap- pointed to wait on the Local Government Board about the Hospital plans had presented their report.—The minutes were approved, on the motion of Mr. TAYLOR, seconded by Mr. HANDLEY. FINANCE: THE UNFAIR SURCHARGE ON MR. NORMAN

AND MR. LYON. The Finance Committee's minutes showed tlaat during August £638 15s 4d had been received, including £659 14s 5d general district rate, and £3 from Messrs. Lyon and Nor- man, being surcharges made by the Local Government auditor in accounts for the year ending March 25th, 1880.— Mr. NORMAN said he was a little grieved in respect to the surcharge of .23, of which he had had to pay £3os and Mr. Lyon the other 30s. He considered it very wrong that either himself or that gentleman should have been sur- charged with the amount. If they had done no good he should have considered it perfectly right they should have been surcharged with the sum, which was the amount of expenses incurred whilst visiting London upon a deputation to Enston station, with the object of getting the railway fares between Liverpool and Runcorn reduced. The result of the journey to London was a reduction of 3d made in the fare to Liverpool. making the cost of the double journey 3d less. This reduction must have caused hundreds of pounds a year to the ratepayers of Runcorn, and he thought it very hard that gentlemen should give their time in this manner for the benefit of the town and then be surcharged. In con- clusion, he had only to state that the money had been paid into the bank. He had pleasure in moving the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Bitiscos seconded the motion.—Dr. Mc- DOVGALL said he was not at all sorry that the Government auditor had gone through a process which might, metapho- rically, be described as extracting the teeth of certain gentlemen, though he must admit he regretted that the gentlemen concerned in this particular case had had to pass through such a process. Perhaps the success which had been made might prove a warning to other gentlemen. If Mr. Norman cared to appeal to the public on this particular question, he had no doubt that they would pay the costs of the "extraction." (Laughter.)—The resolution for the adoption of the minutes was then passed. THE PUBLIC LIBRARY: A CHEERING STATEMENT. The Public Library Committee, of which Dr. McDougall had been appointed chairman, reported that they had an I intergiew with the Literary Institute Committee, who pro- posed to hand over to the Commissioners unconditionally, the Runcorn Library, containing about 800 to 1,000 books, and to sell to the Commissioners their own books (number- ing about 300), and their furniture and effects, at a reduc- tion. The Board then appointed the committees for the ensuing year, as follows : CANAL BOATS AND HOSPITAL..—Messrs. Taylor, Briscoe, Lyon, Handley, Norman, Whittaker, Meadowcroft, and P. Speakman. GENERAL PURPOSES CoststyrrEn.—Messrs. McDougall, ffazlehurst, Briscoe, Lake, Williams, Norman, Lyon, and Speakman. FINANCE COMMITTEE.—Messrs. Lyon, J. J. Speakman, Fisher, Handley, Norman, Briscoe, Hazlehurst, and Shaw. FREEHOLDERS' BIGHTS.—Messrs. Norman, Shaw, Whitta- ker, Fisher, Williams, P. Speakman, and Collier. PUBLIC LIBRARY.—Messrs. McDougall, Norman, Shaw, Briscoe, and HialehßlSl. HIGHWAY AND SANITARY.—This committee consists of the whole Board.

UNJUST MEASURES.—ThOIIaaS Holland, of Warrington, was summoned for having had in his possession, in Runcorn market, a pint and a quart naeasnie which were unjust.— Superintendent Williamson gave evidence as to seizing the measures, and said the quart was a fourth of a gill deficient and the pent an eighth.—Defendaut said he was not at the stall at the time when the alleged offence was committed.— The Chairman said defendant had rendered himself liable to a fine of £5. He would be fined 10s. and costs. The measures were ordered to .be forfeited. MORE POOR RATE DEFAULTERS.—Mr. Sutton, assistant overseer, summoned nine people for non-payment of poor rates, and obtained orders for payment in each case. IeVEDNESDAY.—Bef ore Mr. S. B. Chadwick. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A WESTON YOUNG MAN.— Charles Farndale, a rather good looking young man, employed as a weigher at Weston works, and son 0 Mr. W. M. Farndale, custom house officer, Runcorn, was charged on remand with criminally assaulting a girl about 15 years of age, named Emily Johnson.—Mr. Swift, sen., appeared for the defence.—Complainant, who did not know her age, said she lived with her parents at Clifton. Prisoner had lodged with them about five weeks, but had left before the day of the alleged offence,—the 22nd ultimo. On that afternoon, her mother went to Frodsham about half-past two, and at half.past three Ferndale came to the dwelling and said be wanted his flannel singlet and drawers. She told him that he could not have anything out of the house whilst her father was away. He then took hold of her and carried her upstairs, but she managed to escape and get away. He a second time carried her upstairs and assaulted her. He was in the house from half-past three to a quarter to five. She resisted him whilst he was carrying her up the stairs. She went out after prisoner had left and saw a Mrs. Dids- bury, but did not tell her what had taken place, although the woman asked her what she was crying about. Her mother returned home about seven o'clock but she did not say any- thing to her, as she was frightened; neither did she tell her ' father. On the following Friday she spoke to her mother upon the subject.—ln cross-examination witness said she had been away from home at Chester for 12 months, and Birkenhead seven weeks. home, was turned away at Chester. Though the prisoner had left their house before the day of the offence, he had not taken his box. As soon as her mother returned she went upstairs into the lodgers' room and asked who had been there. She at first said "Nobody," but afterwards stated that the prisoner and a Mrs. Clarke, who was a neighbour, had been there. On the night of the offence the prisoner slept at the house with another lodger. Between the Tuesday and the following Friday her mother found out that what she had said about Mrs. Clarke was a lie, and thrashed witness for making the statement. She then admitted to her mother that prisoner had assaulted her.—Dr. McDougall gave medical evidence. —Ellen Joynson, the mother of complainant, was next called.—Betsy Foster, the wife of a neighbour, said that if complainant had knocked at the wall she could have heard her. In fact, she had frequently done so on former occa- sions.—P.C. Cooper proved the apprehension of the prisoner. —Mr. Swift made a long speech for the defence, and con- tended that but for the observations of the mother the case would never have been heard of.—The magistrate said he did not consider the evidence of such a character as to justify sending the case for trial, and discharged the prisoner. - - - -
THURSDAY.—Before Mr. S. B. Chadwick.

- _ THE Casu Box ROBBERY OF £45. Edward Cawfield, aged about 43, said to be a well-known Birmingham thief, was brought up on remand charged with stealing £lO, the moneys of Mrs. Sarah Evans, High-street, and £45 and a cash box, the property of Mr. George Saunders, of the Fleet- wood Arms, Church-street. The prisoner was first given into custody owing to a married woman with whom he had formed au immoral intimacy at Liverpool, having informed Superintendent Williamson that she was prepared to give evidence implicating him in both robberies. She stated that she was with the prisoner at the time he entered Mrs. Evan's shop, and during the course of some conversation between them' he told her he had stolen £lO whilst there. At a later date he and another man known by the euphonious name of "Puss-in-Boots," went off to Runcorn, and on their return to Liverpool they each showed a large number of sovereigns, saying they had got them at a place not far from the shop where the £lO was obtained. The woman said she would attend the Runcorn court, but on the prisoner being brought up the second time, she did not appear, and the Liverpool police telegraphed that they were unable to find her. Prisoner was again remanded, and on Wednesday the Liverpool police succeeded in finding the woman, and sent her off by train from the city, but as she did not meet P.C. Bossons, who was sent to the station to receive her, it is conjectured she got out at Edge Hill station and decamped, as she has not since been seen. On the prisoner being placed in the dock on Thursday morning, Superintendent Williamson stated that, under the circumstances, he was unable to go on with the charges; and the magistrates then set Cawfield at liberty. He was next charged, under the named of Edward Sharp alias Clayton, with breaking out of Her Majesty's prison at Ruthin, on the borders of North Wales, wheru he was lawfully detained, on the 10th of June, 1873.—Mr. James Walmsley, governor of the gaol, gave evidence to the effect that on the 9th of June, 1873, he had Sharp in custody at Ruthin, he having been convicted at the spring assizes at that town in March of the same year, and sentenced to 12 months' hard labour. During the night of the 10th June, in the same year, prisoner managed to make his escape from gaol, and as a piece of rope was after- wards found attached to the wall, it was supposed he had got away by the aid of it. Witness said he had been authorised to prosecute the prisoner for the offence by the Prison Com- missioners. He, therefore asked the magistrateto remand Sharp, so that he might tale him to Ruthin to be dealt with. div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

WINSFORD ToWN MISSION.—On Sunday last the Rev. James Wright, from Redruth, Cornwall, the newly appointed minister for the Winsford and SandbAck Circuit, preached on behalf of the Town Mission, in the High-street Free Methodist Chapel. A good collection was the result. SALT TRADE, WINSFORD.—The demand weakens with the advance of the season. Brine has been less scarce, and the make active, consequently prices have dropped, but the natural remedy has already begun to operate, namely, stop- page of pans. Freights have risen to all parts except the

east. BIBLE SOCIETY, WINSFORD.—A meeting of the Winston" 1 branch of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held in the Board School. Over, on Wednesday evening, when Mr. Joseph Slater, of Woodford, took the chair, and the Rev. Mr. Symmons attended on behalf of the parent society. There was a fair interest shown. Mr. Symmans delivered an excellent speech. Mr. Slater and the Revs. W. J. Hopper 1 and H. C. Reader also addressed the meeting, and a collec- tion was made at the close. QUARTERLY MEETING OF THE WINSFORD CIRCUIT.— The quarterly meeting of the Winsford and Sandbach United Methodist Free Church was held at Middlewich, in the Newton Bank Chapel, on Monday. There was a good attendonce of preachers, leaders, stewards, Sz.c., presided over by the Rev. W. J. Hopper, superintendent of the circuit. The financial arrangements and conditions having been pat on a very satisfactory footing and all the routine business of the churches attended to, the brethren spent a profitable two hours in a discussion on the interests of the weaker parts of the circuit, and the best means of reasonably expecting a successful change, Middlewich, Over, Weaver, and Clive desPrving the best attention. The following appointments weie made: —Plan Committee, Messrs. Cook, Allen, Oakes, and the Circuit ministers ; representatives to next district meeting at Burslem, the Rev. W. J. Hopper and Mr. J. Cooke. _________

- --...- ROYAL MANCHESTER, LIVERPOOL, AND NORTH LAN- CASHIRE AGILICVLTORAL SOCIETY. On Saturday, the closing day, the weather was again favourable for the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society's show, held in Feniscliffe Meadow, Witton Park, Blackburn. There was some reason to fear rain in the morning, as the sky was overcast with threatening clouds, and-a sharp shower fell soon after ten o'clock, but there was soon an improvement, and the remainder of the day was fine. The mills were stopped, but there was not so large an attendance as might reasonably have been expected on the shilling day under the circumstances. Including ticket holders, there would be a total of about 14,000 visitors to the show ground. The several events in the programme for the day excited considerable interest, which was especially noticeable in connection with the sheep dog trials, and the horse leaping. Between eleven and twelve o'clock the horses and cattle to which prizes had been awarded were paraded in the judging ring for the inspection of the visi- tors by whom the enclosure was surrounded, and at one o'clock the judging of the harriers took place, followed an hour later by the award of prizes for driving horses and , ponies in harness, and subsequently the horse leaping com- petitions. At two o'clock the final trials of sheep dogs in the park, in a ieW of patrone of the show standing on the banks of the DaTINTII, commenced, and the interest in them I increased as the contest neared the close. The operations 1 of butter making, Stc., in the working dairy were watched with great attentioa by a large number of persons, and the , live stock, implements, and machinery were insp'ected with evident interest.

div.head: NEW BOUNDARIES.
div.p: THE NEW BOUNDARIES.

The LAW CLERK said it would be necessary for the Board to apply to the Local Government Board for a provisional order for the proposed alterations in the area of the district. —Dr. MCDOUGALL : Have you had a communication from the Local Government Board that they agree to the pro- posed changes ?—The Law CLERK: No; but we must not allow that to interfere with our proceeding. We shall have to give notice before the 15th October.—Dr. MCDOUGALL thought they ought to hear the result of the enquiry at Frodsham before they took any steps to apply for a provi- sional order. rhere would be time at the next meeting to give notice.—lt was decided that the question be referred to the Highway and Sanitary Committee, on the motion of Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Dr. McDounALL. THE SEWER FLAN. In answer to remarks from various members, the Scrn- YEYOR said it was quite true that there was a plan in exis- tence of the sewers of the town. It was in course of com- pletion but there was a great deal of the new part of the town which required to be put upon it yet. THE TIME OF MEETING. The CHAIRMAN said he thought another day of meeting would be preferable to Monday, when they met at 10-30 in the forenoon. He thought Tuesday would be a much better day.—Dr. MoDouGALL suggested seven o'clock on the first Monday in each month. He moved, and Mr. DilEanowcnoFT seconded, a motion to that effect.—Seven members voted in its favour and seven against.—The Chairman gave his casting vote against the resolution, and it was declared lost, amid laughter. This conclude 3 the proceedings.

THE WINTER ASSIZES.—By three several Orders in Council, dated Holyrood, 26th ult., it is ordered, first, that the counties of Cumberland and Westmorland, for the pur- poses of the next winter assizes. be united to form one county, and that the assizes to be held at Carlisle; second, that the Northern and Salford Divisions of the county of Lancaster form one county, the assizes to be held in Man- chester; and third, that the counties of Chester, Mont- gomery, Merioueth, Carnarvon, Anglesea, Denbigh, and Flint be also one county, the assizes to be held at Chester. A BOY SWALLOWING POISON AT ST. IaRLENS.-00. Saturday evening a little boy, five years of age, named Jas. Shepherd, residing with his parents in Water-street, swal- lowed a quantity of liquid poison which he obtained from a shelf in the cupboard. The mother went out of the house for a short time and it appears whilst she was out the lad climbed to the time, from which be got a bottle of atropia used by the father for his eyes, and drank a portion of the contents of the bottle. The boy finding the liquid had a different taste to that which he anticipated began to cry, and assistance soon arrived. It was then discovered by the neighbours that the boy had swallowed some poison, and he was carried to the surgery of Drs. Twyford and Jamison in Church-street, followed by a crowd of people. Emetics were administered at intervals within the space of two hours, and vomiting was caused, and at the expiration of that time the boy was taken home in a weakly condition.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS

At the fortnightly meeting, held on Tuesday, Mr. John Ashton presided, and there were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. T. Norman, William Fisher, William Handley, John Darbyshire, John Highfield, Henry Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). MR. BOLEBTIRN TAKES. DR. MC DOIJGALL TO TASK. A letter was read from the Local Government Board, dated the 25th ult., forwarding the copy of a communication which had been addressed to them the by Mr. H. Coleburn, vaccination officer for the Runcorn district, together with the certificates of vaccination therein referred to. They re- quested that such certificates might be returned to them, and also asked that the guardians would be good enough to , obtain and forward them any explanation which Dr. McDougall. the public vaccinator of the district, might wish J to offer. The following is a copy of the letter referred to: —" Runcorn, August 8, 1881. My Lords and Gentlemen,— Enclosed I send 21 medical certificates of successful vaccina- tion for your perusal, which appeared to me ' to de informally signed, and beg to say that I await your instructions in reference to the same, in order that I may be enabled to enter the particulars thereof in , column 12 of the vaccination register. Your lordships will observe that a considerable length of time has passed since the date of the certificates, but this is accounted for on my part from the fact that I have been waiting for the instruc- tions given by Mr. Linaker, clerk to the Board of Guardians, to Mr. McDougall, the public vaccinator, to be carried out. Mr. Lisaker's letter to me, and a copy of the one sent by him to Mr. McDougall I also enclose. I delivered the certi- ficates with others at the end of the then quarter to Mr. Linaker, but they were returned to me. When Dr. Board,l the vaccination inspector, visited me in January last,l men- tioned the matter te him, and I believe he took two of the I certificates with him, which makes a total of 28. I had appended notes to the certificates, which will explain to to your lordships how they have been dealt with. I may add that Mr. McDougall was from home for about a fort- night in June of last year, and Mr. Maxwell attended to his practice and to the vaccination during his absence.—l am, my lords and gentlemen, your most obedient servant, HENRY COLEBURN, Vaccination Officer."—.The Clerk gave an !x- -planation to the Board on the matter, to the following effect :—ln June 1880, Dr. McDougall wrote to the guar- dians that he was going away for a change of air, and saying he had appointed Dr. Maxwell, a duly qualified man, as his substitute, under the supervision of Dr. Carruthers. The guardians passed a resolution approving of the arrange- ments made by Dr. McDougall fcr the performance of his duties during his absence. In the following month the clerk received a complaint from Mr. Coleburn, the vaccina- tion officer, that 23 certificates had been signed by Dr. Maxwell, and as he had not been appointed as deputy vaccination officer. he did not approve of it. The matter was mentioned to Dr. Beard, inspector of vaccination, but he did not see fit to take any steps in regard to it. The clerk also wrote to Dr. McDougall upon the subject, and that gentleman replied that he had appointed Dr. Maxwell under the terms of his contract with the guar- dians. With that explanation the clerk was perfectly satisfied, and had forwarded it to the Local Government Board, and now awaited their reply.—Mr. NORMAN: Have we not had application after application for different men to be appointed in the place of Dr.-Weaver? I think it is 'a very wrong thing indeed.—Mr. HANDLEY : I suppose it was a case of absence from accident ? The CLERK: Yes, but Dr. McDomall has power under his contract to appoint any duly qualified man.—Mr. HANDLEY : I think that Mr. Cole- burn has been very officious.—Mr. NORMAN : I think so, too. I should wait for a reply.—The CLERK: It would perhaps be as well if Dr. McDougall were to acknowledge the receipt of the letter from the Local Government Board.—The dis- cussion then dropped. THE COST OF THE HOSPITAL EXTENSION. It was decided to borrow the sum of £2,400 at four per cent. for 20 years from the Royal Exchange Insurance Co., on account of hospital extension.

ANNUAL PRIZE MEETING OF THE RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS. The 22nd annual prize meeting of the F and G (Runcorn companies of the 2nd Cheshire Rifle Volunteer Corps, took place on their range on Saturday last. The money given in prizes amounted to about £3O, and there was also a great number of articles, ranging in value from 3s. to a guinea There were no fewer than 104 contributors to the list of prizes, 71 of whom subscribed money, while the remaining 33 gave articles of various descriptions. The donors include the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton, M.P., E. Jones, Esq., of The Elms, Daresbury ; Lieut.-Col. Ashton, Captain C. W. Dewhurst, the principal inhabitants of the town, and gentry of the surrounding district. The weather throughout the day was fine, but the atmospherical conditions were not altogether conducive to good shooting. There was a gentle breeze blowing from the right front, which at times was very unsteady, but it, was the teacherous light that upset the cal- culation of many a competitor, and brought him to grief at the long distances. The ranges were 200, 500, and 600 yards for the Company prizes; 200 and 300 yards, for the Recruits', seven rounds at each range; 200 and 500 yards for the Marksmen's prizes, five rounds at each range ; Wimbledon targets and scoring, any position. There were some remarkably good scores made at the 200 yards range, Sergeant Moore putting on 34 out of a possible 35; Private T. Kay, 28; and Sergeant Harvey, 28. The entire arrange- ments were verfy satisfactorily carried out by the Shooting Committee, who have an energetic and indefatigable hon. secretary in Sergeant J. Poole. Captain C. W. Hazlehurst was on the ground during the competitions. The distribu- tion of prizes will take place in the Runcorn Public Hall, ' when the usual miscellaneous entertainment will be given, which, we understand, will be of a first-rate quality, several ; well-known artistes having already promised their services. ROYAL VISIT TO LrvEnPoOL.—The opening of an important extension of the Liverpool dock system was made the occasion, on Thursday, of an imposing demonstration the central figures in which were the Prince and Princess of Wales, the former of whom opened one dock whilst the latter named a second the "Alexandra." The town was handsomely decorated, and the reception given to the Royal visitors was most enthusiastic. Their Royal Highnesses, were entertained at lunch by the Dock Company, and were subsequently presented with an address on behalf of the City. Speaking at the luncheon the Prince referred to the great progress made by the City of Liverpool during the present century, and gave some particulars with regard to the growth of the dock system. The Royal party left I...verpoel list night for Abergeldie. They started at mid- night by ,oecial train, and were to reach Carlisle at 3-35 this morn ,g, the route, after a short stay at the border city, being con aued to Ballater, whence the Royal party drive to Aberget lie, which will be reached early in the afternoon. The Prince and Princess of Wales are expected to remain about a month in the Highlands.

div.head: PFCEPTION OF MR. GARNETT AT
div.p: PFCEPTION OF MR. GARNETT AT

SALFORD. On the e:ening of the let bast. Mr. Charles Garnett, of Runcorn, who has been appointed Wesleyan Methodist missionary at Salford, was welcomed at a public meeting .The gathering was held in the large schoolroom connected with the chapel, which is the centre uf Mr. Garnett's work. Previous to the meeting about 250 of the friends sat down to tea. The Rev. Walford Green, superintendent of the Radnor-street circuit, presided at the meeting,and wee sup- ported on the platform by the Revs. John Colwell, ministerial secretary of the mission T. GaNand Hartley. and Mr. T. Willshaw, hon. secretary of the mission, and other friends. After devotional exercises, Mr. Green explained ' that henceforth old George-street Chapel was to be the centre of home mission work in that district. (Applause.) The chapel was a large and commodious one, but the neigh- bourhood was densely populated, and. he saw no reason why it should not soon be filled with worshippers. The Execu- tive had, he was happy to say, appointed Mr. Charles Garnett as the Evangelist, and he had reason to believe that he would fulfil their expectations, high as they probably were. He earnestly contended that the old town chapels, where the congregations had fallen off in consequence of removals, should be made the centre of earnest Christian evangelisation, and thus practically solve the two-fold pro- i blem which was troubling so many devoted Christians now- a-days, viz., "How to reach the masses," and how at the same time to fill the once thronged but now, in many cases, neglected town chapels. (Applause.)—Mr. Willshaw ex- plained the relation in which Mr. Garnett would stand to the church and congregation, and observed that the present step would be regarded as a kind of experiment, and if it succeeded, as he believed it would, the committee would be encouraged to adopt the same plan in connection with other places of worship in the district. (Applause.)—After a few earnest words of exhortation from the Rev. T. G. Hartley, the Chairman introduced Mr. Garnett to the meeting amid cheers. He remarked that he was sure they would give Mr. Garnett a most cordial welcome, and that with the blessing of God the union then consummated would be pro- ductive of great and lasting good—Mr. Garnett, in respond- ing, said: I thank you, Mr. Chairman, and dear friends, for your cordial welcome. You may be sure that I am greatly encouraged by it. Coming amongst you as a perfect stranger, I must say I already feel quite at home; and I account for in this way. lam a Wesleyan Methodist, of the primitive type, and I find many of you are the same. (Applause.) For my own part, when I meet a man, I believe in a hearty salutation, and a. vigorous shake of the hand, as if we meant it—(laughter)—and in a prayer meeting, or other religious gathering, I like a good response now and then. It does no one any harm, and I find most people enjoy it. lam glad that my relation to the members of society has been clearly defined. I oome among you not as your pastor or teacher so much as your evangelist and missionary. My work is not in the church, but out among the people. Already I am deeply impressed with the religious indifference of the people, and with the flagrant immorality of some. With very many life is but a pitiless struggle for the means of a joyless ex- istence. and all are sinful and sad. I propose in the first place to lay the foundation of my work in the confidence and affection of the people.. The way to reach the masses is to deal with individuals. I want to know them, their difficulties, their sorrows, their sins, their hindrances. Then I can sympathise with them and help them, then I can adapt myself and my message to them. (Applause.) I also want them to know me. Unless we have the confidence of the people we can really do little or nothing for them. They are suspicious and critical in their way, and we must try to show them the beauty of goodness and the power of vital religion. They must believe in us as well as in Christianity. Indeed, what is Christianity but embodied living holiness? (Applause.) Mr. Garnett also dwelt upon the power on the pure gospel and other kindred topics, and spoke hopefully of his prospects there.—After several other short speeches the meeting, which was of a most enjoyable character, terminated.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held on Wed- y, there being present Aldermen Johnson, Gamble, Cook, and Mcßride; Councillors J. C. Gamble, Twvford, Fisher, Cook, Baxter, Massey, Foster, Walker, Hanson, Bishop, Belsher, Wilcock, Brook, Owen, and W. W. Pilk- ington. A BOROUGH BENCH FOR ST. HELENS. Mr. MA.SOEY moved, "That the time has now arrived when it is necessary that a borough bench be appointed for St. Helens, and that this Council petition the Crownto make such appointment." He did not think it necessary to repeat his arguments at very great length. He was encouraged to make this motion a second time for the reason that at the Council meeting it was brought forward it was only lost by ' the casting vote of the Mayor, and also by reason of a motion which was attempted to be moved by Mr. Councillor Windle Pilkington which admitted the great charges against the county magistrate; and perhaps' admitted without any intention on his part that there had been serious delays in 1 the administration of justice; that great inconvenience to suitors had been caused through a deficiency of magistratesl in the magistrates' court. If that were so it seemed almostl, impossible that anyone could be found that day—and he 1 hoped it would be impossible—to oppose his motion. The evil had been admitted, and it ought to be remedied. Since his last motiort six months had expired, and the evil all along had been allowed Ito exist. The evil being ad- mitted one would have thought that the county magistrates would have taken some steps to remedy it, but they had not done so. They had had six months in which to turn them- selves round and look for eligible candidates for the position, but not finding amongst their own class men capable of dis- charging the duties, they were still desirous of keeping the blameable state of things in static quo. Nobody could deny , the evil which existed through a want of magistrates. He 1 did not want to multiply them, but there were many in- stances which showed a discreditable state of things. He commenced to read a paragraph which appeared in one of the ' local papers, but was interrupted by Mr. Alderman GAMBLE who said it was not usual to read extracts from newspapers, especially when some, of the Council believed that the writer of the paragraph was the same gentleman I who read them. Mr. MASSEY (laughing) : Oh, that is quite a mistake. I scarcely think it is necessary to answer that, because it is customary in all assemblies like this to read extracts from papers. lam not the writer of the paragraph which said that a number of cases had to be adjourned on account of there being only one magistrate present, and some of those cases were very important ones. It must be patent to every one that a state of things like this ought not to be allowed to exist. But still the matter went on, and only on Monday last some inconvenience was caused, , and cases had to be adjourned, thus wasting the time of ' suitors and advocates. This state of things, of course, worked a great hardship. Suppose a workingman went to the court with five or six witnesses, and engaged a solicitor to ad- vocate his case. He went prepared with his witnesses to I give his testimony, but there were not two magistrates pre- sent. The consequence was the case had to be adjourned, the man and his witnesses lost their day's work, and were I told to come another day. Frequently, within his own ex- perience, witnesses would not come back again, and the pro- I cess of the court was not sufficient to get them there, becausel they could not afford to lose a day's work.l How long was such a state of things to continue? It was for that Council to watch over thp interests of the borough very particularly and very zealously. Was it to the in- tereets of the borough that that state of things should go on They had no guarantee that it would not continue, and he asked the Council to take what the law said it ought to take—take the matter into its own hands, and petition the- Crown for the appointment of its own magistrates. The Act of Parliament contemplated that the time would at no distant datearrive when they would have a bench of borough magistrates. The Municipal Corporations Act specially invited corporations to avail themselves of the provisions of that Act, and get the appointment of borough magistrates. He could not see what possible objection there could be. Why were the county magistrates so desirous of having it in their own hands, and what was it that made them so jealous ? They were told on the last occasion that some of the county magi- strates would not sit on the bench with borough magistrates. He could not see any difference, and ventured to assert dis- tinctly that there were gentlemen in St. Helens who would be an ornament to the bench, who had, the confidence of their fellow townsmen, and are quite as capable of administering justice in that court as any magistrate on the bench. It was rather a slander on that Council for anyone to say that there was not a member fit to sit with a county magistrate. Surely some members of the Council must have in their minds many gentlemen who by position, and the confidence placed in them, were pre-eminently fitted for the discharge of those duties which the position of amagistrate demanded. If they had had borough magistrates sitting on a recent case affect- ing the rights of property owner?, a different result would have been arrived at, and would had been in accordance with every principle of justice and propriety. The fees in the county magistrates court were very much higher than in the borough court; for instance, a man applying for a summons would have to pay five or six shillings for it, but under the other system half-a-crown or three shillings, so that there- would be a tremendous saving to the suitors in court which was absolutely neces- sary, particularly when wages were low. It was not only necessary, but it was desirable in every sense of the word that cheap justice should be dealt out to the inhabitants. The fees were at present too high and ought to be altered. He need scarcely refer to what was in vogue in other towns. It had been mentioned before that nearly every town, in fact every town of any importance round about St. Helens had its own borough bench of magistrates. The system worked well, and why should it not work well in St. Helens?' —Mr. BROOK seconded Mr. Massey's motion, and remarked that the arguments put forward on former occasions were convincing enough for anyone that the time had arrived when St. Helens, with its 60,000 inhabitants, should have a borough bench of magistrates.—Alderman GAMBLE rose to I move an amendment, "That the time has now arrived when it is necessary that additional magistrates for this division of the county be appointed; and that this Council forthwith memorialise the Lord-Lieutenant to make such additional , appointments." This was almost the same resolution which , was attempted by Major Pilkington when the matter was ' before the Council on anothet occasion, and not as Mr. Massey 1 had stated, before the Council had determined to reject his motion, but afterwards. He did not for a moment wish to make little of the inconvenience, and perhaps discreditable inconvenience, to those who visit the magistrates' court, and somebody was to blame for it. Those who attended on Fri- days were not to blame. He would ask the Coun- cil not to decide in alteration of the kind proposed without full consideration. The difficulty possibly might be met by the appointment of a borough bench. It might be that the members of the borough magistracy would attend more regularly; probably they would. But he must remind them that they did not get on the borough bench quite the same class of gentlemen as were to be found on the county bench. Besides that, the borough magistrates would not have the right of sending a representative to the general quarter sessions, and the annual sessions of the peace, at which the business on the county was carried on. St. Helens would therefore be unrepresentsd. There would be another inconvenience. They would have to hold ses- sions both for the borough and county. The district of the petty sessional division including part of Eccleston, the whole of the outlying districts of Eecleston, with the ex- ception of about thirty acres at the Four-lane Ends, which belonged to Prescot division • that part of Windle which was immediately beyond Mr. 'Ausdell's park, but very close to them, and in fact, part of the town; Dentons Green, and where he lived, Moss-bank, and all that neighbourhood, all of which would be excluded the right to the borough bench, and would have to go to the sessions which would be held once a fortnight or so, or sent to Prescot, which he supposed was not pro- bable. Besides those districts, Bold and Rainford would share similarly. He thought those were the objections to having a borough bench. He had told them he did not want to make little of the inconvenience of suitors, and he remembered very distinctly the reasons pat forward by Mr Swift in a very eloquent manner indeed why St. Helens should maintain its position as a borough, and claim its 1 right, which it undoubtedly had, of leaving magistrates of its own. But he still felt that if they were properly sup- plied with county magistrates it would be better. He could not help feeling that the appointment of a borough bench I would be followed by borough police; and that was very possible indeed. The fees of the county, of course, were 1 high, but they had no guarantee that they would be lower under the new system.—Mr. BAXTER seconded Alderman , Gamble's amendment. If they adopted Mr. Massey's reso- lution they would be taking a very important step. He believed there were a great many things to be said in favour of a borough bench, and no doubt it would come in time; but the time had not yet arrived. div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

At the meeting of this Board on Thursday, at the Work- house, VVhiston, Mr. John Fidler presided. There were also present the Rev. J. Barnacle, Messrs. J. Penketh, J. T. Hall, T. Sadler, W. Gerrard, Joseph Jackson, J. Buckley, J. Ran- son, W. Swift, J. Fisher, W. Birchall, T. Dobell, T. Eatock, J. Lowe, E. Syder, J. Leatherharrow, and J. Kenwright with Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk.

div.head: EXCLUSION or A REPORTER.
div.p: THE EXCLUSION or A REPORTER.

The CLERK read a record of the proceedings at the last meeting, which contained a minute to the effect that the reporter who was forcibly ejected should be excluded from all future meetings of the Board. WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT. Mr. BICKNELL, workhouse master, reported that the number of inmates in the house on the last day of this week was 452, as compared with 465 in the preceding week, and 429 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 141 boys and girls. Mr. and Mrs. Scannell entered upon their duties as porter and portress on the 29th August. There were four pigs on the Workhouse farm that had the foot- and-mouth disease. There was one case of smallpox in the hospital—The CLERK stated that he had seen Mr. Welsby, who had informed him that the pigs were getting better.

div.head: INFECTIOUS HOSPITAL FOR WIDNES.
div.p: INFECTIOUS HOSPITAL FOR WIDNES.

----- The CLERK said he had that morning received a letter from the Widnes Local Board, after considerable pressure, intimating that the Board had definitely settled on having a hospital for the treatment of infectious diseases arising in the town, as soon as the pressing matters in hand had been settled. OFFER OF THE MASTER TO RE—COMMENCE THE LUNCHEON. The Clerk was proceeding to read a letter from the Master relative to the luncheon question, when he was in- terrupted by the CHAIRMAN, who exclaimed: Don't read it through.—Mr. JACKSON : Don't entertain it further. Let it lie on the table.—Several members, however, suggested that it should be read, and the Clerk read as follows :—" I am now in a position to re-commence the usual luncheon, and if it is the wish of the majority of Guardians, I shall be glad to do so next Board day. I shall be much obliged if you will ascertain the pleasure of the Guardians in the matter." —The CHAIRMAN : Gentlemen, what is your pleasure ? Mr. LEATHERBARROW : That no dinners or luncheons be provided in the Workhouse.—Mr. HALL considered it very unwise on the part of the Master to send the Board such a letter after the manner in which he had treated them. He did not know whether the Master thought them " dummies " or not, but it was a very unwise letter.—Rev. Mr.BarceacLE said it seemed to him the Guardians would be acting very unwisely if they accepted the kindness of the Master. (Hear, hear.)—lt was resolved, on the motion of Mr. LEATHERBARROW, seconded by Mr. GERRARD, that no lun- cheons be provided in the Workhouse for the Guardians. A SINGULAR AFFAIR. A discussion took place respecting the circumstances of the re-admission into the Workhouse of the woman Griffin, who was sent out of the house a few weeks ago by the Revision Committee, and whose expulsion caused the Guardians' dinners to be diseontinued.—Mr. HALL remarked that the avonlan came into the Workhouse on the 24th Feb., 1881, and was sent into the hospital by the doctor, but how long she remained there he could not say. However, she became a servant—a cook he supposed, although they had a man whom they paid to cook for the inmates. When the revision was made, the committee resolved that all able- bodied persons, male and female, who had no ties should leave the Workhouse. The committee considered that the woman Griffin was an able-bodied person, and had no right in the house. She left the house, and then they were told by the Master that they could not have their luncheon. He would like to know whet the woman had got to do with pro- viding the Guardians' luncheon. Nothing whatever. They had a cook, specially paid. to cook for them. The woman had come back again, and the Master said he was now prepared to provide luncheon. There were a score of women in the house who could do the work this woman had done. If the Guardians could not have luncheon at the workhouse without this woman, they had better do without it. Dr. McNicoll had given a certificate for palpi- tation at the heart, and the relieving officer knowing nothing about the woman, had given her an order for admission to the house. He (Mr. Hall) had had a conversation with Dr. Hall, the medical officer of the house, who informed him that he would not send the woman to the hospital as it was not a case for the hospital,—in fact, tbat it was not a case for the workhouse at all. Everybody had palpitation to a certain extent, and if they took in such cases they would soon have to build a new workhouse —Mr. LOWE thought that if the woman was able-bodied and capable of providing the Guardians' dinners, she should be sent out at once.—lt was resolved, on the motion of Mr. RANSON, seconded by Mr. JACKSON, that the woman be discharged at once.
